docs.title: dagger-build
docs.text:
Shared Go tooling for building and testing Osixia container images with Dagger. Each image project keeps its own build executable, image matrix and integration tests; dagger-build provides the common jobs and CLI.

It is a Go library using the standalone Dagger SDK, rather than a standalone application or a native Dagger module. It requires Go 1.26.1 or newer and uses Dagger SDK/engine 0.21.10.

docs.title: ⚡ Try it in an existing project
docs.text:
You need Go and a running Docker engine for the default local Dagger setup. From a checkout of container-baseimage:

cd build
go run . --help
go run . job test ../Dockerfile --target base --distributions debian --arches amd64

Use --arches arm64 on an ARM64 runner. Limiting the architecture and distribution keeps the first run small. The SDK downloads the matching Dagger CLI when it connects.

job test builds the images and runs the tests; it does not publish images. The default test checks that the image's --version output matches its generated image name and tag. The consuming project can add its own checks.

docs.title: 🔧 Use it in your own project
docs.text:
Create a Go build program in your project's build/ directory. Add a dependency pinned to an existing tag or commit:

go get github.com/osixia/dagger-build@<existing-tag-or-commit>

The program configures an image, then runs the shared CLI:

package main

import (
    "context"
    "os"

    "github.com/osixia/dagger-build/cmd"
    "github.com/osixia/dagger-build/config"
)

func main() {
    image := &config.Image{
        BaseImage:    "debian:trixie-slim",
        Distribution: config.Debian,
        Name:         "example/my-image",
        TagPrefixes:  []string{"debian"},
    }
    config.Images = []*config.Image{image}
    config.DefaultImage = image
    config.ProjectGithubRepo = &config.GithubRepo{
        Organization: "example",
        Project:      "my-image",
    }
    if err := cmd.Run(context.Background()); err != nil {
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

Your Dockerfile must accept the BASE_IMAGE and IMAGE build arguments. For the default test, its entrypoint must print <image-name>:<generated-tag> when called with --version.

docs.title: 🧪 Common commands
docs.text:
Run these from the consuming project's build directory:

Command What it does go run . job build ../Dockerfile Build the configured images go run . job test ../Dockerfile Build and test, using the project's test hook go run . job test ../Dockerfile --export /usr/sbin/container --export-to ../bin Also export a binary from the default image go run . job test ../Dockerfile --oci-export-to ../oci Export images as OCI archives for later use

Use --target, --distributions and --arches to select what to build. Use --help on any command for its options.

docs.title: 🏗️ Project tests and CI
docs.text:
To add integration tests, assign job.Test before calling cmd.Run. Call job.DefaultTest first, then run your checks against the returned containers. Keep the fixtures and tests in the consuming project.

For multiple architectures, build and test on native runners, export with --oci-export-to, then collect the archives for the final job with --oci-import-from. Imported images are not tested again before deployment.

The provider github command selects jobs from the GitHub ref. Tag pipelines, job deploy and job publish can push images and change GitHub releases or assets. Use job test for local validation.

docs.title: osixia/baseimage
docs.text:
Debian, Alpine, and Ubuntu container base images designed to build reliable containers quickly.

This image provides a simple, opinionated solution for building single- or multi-process container images with a minimal number of layers and an optimized build process.

It accelerates image development and CI/CD pipelines by offering:

  • Advanced build tools to reduce image layers and maximize Docker layer caching efficiency.
  • A lightweight init system as the container entrypoint, providing enhanced process management, debugging capabilities, and runtime flexibility.
  • Built-in support for multi-process containers. Run all processes within a single container or split them across multiple containers as needed.

Includes non-root container images and supports read-only container environments.

docs.title: Passing Arguments to process.sh
docs.text:
Any argument passed after the image name at runtime is captured by the baseimage and then handled in one of two ways:

  • If at least one service process.sh is run, the same argument list is appended to every running process.sh.
  • If no service process.sh is run, the argument list is treated as a standalone command to execute instead.
  • If no service is run and no command is provided, Bash is started automatically.

Examples:

docker run --rm my-image -- --config /etc/my-app.yml

If my-image has one linked service, its process.sh is executed as:

/container/services/service-1/process.sh --config /etc/my-app.yml

In a multi-process image, the same arguments are passed to every running service process:

docker run --rm my-image -- --verbose

This means:

/container/services/service-a/process.sh --verbose
/container/services/service-b/process.sh --verbose

Use this only when the same runtime arguments make sense for all running services.

docs.title: Controlling Container Lifecycle Steps
docs.text:
The entrypoint lifecycle has three steps:

  1. startup
  2. process
  3. finish

Behavior by step:

  • startup: runs --pre-startup-cmd commands, then every running service startup.sh in service priority order.
  • process: runs --pre-process-cmd commands, then the main command and/or every running service process.sh.
  • finish: runs --pre-finish-cmd commands, then every running service finish.sh in service priority order.
  • exit: always runs --pre-exit-cmd before the container exits.

Useful flags:

  • --skip-startup, --skip-process, --skip-finish
  • --step startup|process|finish
  • --exec service-name
  • --skip service-name
  • --skip-all

Important details:

  • .priority affects install.sh, startup.sh, and finish.sh.
  • .priority does not affect process.sh; all running service processes are started concurrently.
  • --step process runs only the process step and skips startup and finish.
  • If --skip-process is used together with --bash, process services are skipped but Bash still runs.
  • Environment files are loaded before lifecycle pre-commands and service scripts, unless --skip-env-files is used.

docs.title: Running Extra Commands
docs.text: There are two distinct ways to run extra commands.

docs.title: 1. Pre-step commands
docs.text:
Use:

  • --pre-startup-cmd
  • --pre-process-cmd
  • --pre-finish-cmd
  • --pre-exit-cmd

Each flag can be repeated. Commands are split with shell-like parsing, but they are not executed through a shell unless you explicitly call one yourself.

Example:

docker run --rm my-image \
  --pre-startup-cmd 'mkdir -p /run/container/cache' \
  --pre-process-cmd 'sh -c "echo ready > /tmp/health"'

If you need pipes, redirects, shell expansion, or compound shell syntax, wrap the command with sh -c or bash -c.

docs.title: 2. Run a command alongside services
docs.text:
Use:

docker run --rm my-image --bash

This starts Bash in parallel with running service processes.

If no service process is run:

  • arguments after the flags are run as a command
  • --bash can still be used to run Bash alongside that command

This is mainly useful for debugging and container inspection.

docs.title: Running Multi-Process Images in Separate Containers
docs.text:
The same image can be used either as:

  • one multi-process container
  • several single-purpose containers

Use container services link during build to define the default linked services. At runtime, narrow the selection with --exec or remove services with --skip.

Examples:

docker run --rm my-image

Runs all linked services.

docker run --rm my-image --exec nginx

Runs only the nginx service lifecycle.

docker run --rm my-image --exec php-fpm

Runs only the php-fpm service lifecycle.

This pattern is useful when:

  • you want one build artifact but different deployment topologies
  • you want to split a multi-process development image into separate production containers
  • you want to debug one service without starting the others

Keep in mind:

  • startup and finish scripts still run for the services being run only
  • process arguments are shared across all running services
  • restart behavior changes with the number of running process scripts

By default:

  • single running process: restart is disabled
  • multiple running processes: restart is enabled

Override this with --restart=true or --restart=false.

When restart is enabled, a failed process is retried with an exponential backoff delay, starting at 100 milliseconds and capped at 5 seconds. The delay resets after an execution lasting at least 30 seconds. Use --no-restart-delay to disable this delay and retry immediately:

docker run --rm my-image --restart=true --no-restart-delay

--no-restart-delay does not enable restarting on its own and does not change the wait for intentionally stopped processes. Immediate retries can consume significant CPU if a process keeps failing repeatedly.

docs.title: 🧩 How It Works
docs.text:
Quick overview of project files:

osixia-baseimage-example
├── Dockerfile
├── environment
│   └── .env
└── services
    └── service-1
        ├── finish.sh
        ├── install.sh
        ├── process.sh
        └── startup.sh

docs.title: Dockerfile
docs.text:
A typical Dockerfile extending osixia/baseimage usually looks like this:

FROM osixia/baseimage

ARG IMAGE="osixia/baseimage-example:latest"
ENV CONTAINER_IMAGE=${IMAGE}

# Download services required packages or resources
# RUN container packages install --update --clean \
#        [...]
#     && curl -o resources.tar.gz https://[...].tar.gz \
#     && tar -xzf resources.tar.gz \
#     && rm resources.tar.gz

COPY services /container/services

# Install and link services to the entrypoint
RUN container services install \
    && container services link

COPY environment /container/environment

Below is a line-by-line explanation

FROM osixia/baseimage
Create a new build stage from osixia base image.

ARG IMAGE="osixia/multi-process-example"
ENV CONTAINER_IMAGE=${IMAGE}
Define a build-time variable IMAGE and assign its value to the CONTAINER_IMAGE environment variable. This allows the container command to determine the image name, which can be useful for debugging purposes.

To leverage this feature, build the image with the --build-arg option: docker build -t example/my-image:develop --build-arg IMAGE=example/my-image:develop .

# Download services required packages or resources
# RUN container packages install --update --clean \
#        [...]
#     && curl -o resources.tar.gz https://[...].tar.gz \
#     && tar -xzf resources.tar.gz \
#     && rm resources.tar.gz
Uncomment and adapt this stage to download the image service resources required at build time. This can include anything that takes time to download and can be cached to speed up image rebuilds.

The container command provided by osixia/baseimage offers a simple, distribution-agnostic command-line interface to install distribution packages. For example, to install cowsay: container packages install --update --clean cowsay

This command updates the package index, installs cowsay, and cleans the index cache afterward. It works transparently across Debian, Ubuntu, and Alpine.

COPY services /container/services
Copy the services directory into the image at /container/services.

If changes occur in this directory — for example in the install.sh script — only this stage will be re-executed. The resources downloaded in the previous stage will remain cached.

This makes it easier to iterate quickly on service script development.

RUN container services install \
    && container services link
This will execute all non-optional service install.sh scripts and link those services to the entrypoint.

As a result, these services will run by default when the container starts.

COPY environment /container/environment
Finally, copy the environment directory, which defines the default environment variables, into the image at /container/environment.

docs.title: Service Files
docs.text:
This section describes all files used by the container command within a service directory. Additional files may also be included without impacting the service behavior.

The files outlined below are not mandatory.

docs.title: install.sh
docs.text:
This script should exclusively contain instructions for the initial setup of the service.

For improved image construction, all package installations or file downloads should occur within the Dockerfile.

By separating time-intensive download operations from the setup, the docker build cache is utilized effectively. Changes to the install.sh file will not necessitate re-downloading dependencies, as the Dockerfile builder will only execute the service installation script.

Note: The install.sh script executes during the docker build, thus runtime environment variables cannot be used for setup customization. Such customizations are handled in the startup.sh file.

docs.title: startup.sh
docs.text: This script prepares process.sh for execution and tailors the service setup to runtime environment variables.

docs.title: process.sh
docs.text:
This script specifies the command to be executed.

For multi-process images, all process.sh scripts are launched simultaneously. The order defined in the service .priority file is irrelevant.

docs.title: finish.sh
docs.text: This script is executed once process.sh has concluded.

docs.title: .priority
docs.text: The .priority file establishes the sequence in which services install.sh, startup.sh or finish.sh scripts are invoked. The smaller the number, the greater the priority. The default is 500.

docs.title: .stop-signal
docs.text:
This file sets the signal used to stop the service process. The default is SIGTERM. For a graceful Nginx or PHP-FPM shutdown, put SIGQUIT in the file:

SIGQUIT

You can generate it with container generate services nginx --stop-signal SIGQUIT. Keep the application's shutdown timeout within the entrypoint's --kill-all-timeout (default: 15s) and give Docker or Kubernetes a longer termination grace period.

docs.title: .optional
docs.text: This file indicates that the service is optional and is not installed by container services install by default. It can be incorporated later via the container services require service-name command.

docs.title: download.sh
docs.text:
This script is called during container build to download optional service resources.

Example of a Dockerfile using an optional service from a base image:

FROM [...]

# Require and download optional services
RUN container services require service-name \
    && container services download

# Install and link services to the entrypoint
RUN container services install \
    && container services link

docs.title: Service Tags
docs.text:
A service directory may contain a .tags sub-directory. Each file in this directory defines a tag, where the filename is used as the tag name.

Services and their related processes can then be filtered by tag through the services and processes subcommands.

To learn more about tag usage, run container services status --help

docs.title: Environment Files
docs.text:
.env files in the environment directory and any sub-directories are loaded before executing services lifecycle scripts (startup.sh, process.sh, and finish.sh) or entrypoint lifecycle pre-commands. The variables they contain are defined as environment variables in the container.

Files are loaded in alphabetical order, and variables are overwritten if they were already defined in a previous file.

Container environment variables set at runtime override values defined in .env files.

docs.title: Precedence and variable interpolation
docs.text:
Variables already present in the container environment, including those provided with docker run -e, take precedence over environment files. Their values are preserved exactly, including empty values, quotes, newlines, and $ characters.

Within environment files, $VAR and ${VAR} references are expanded using gotenv. Existing container environment variables can be used to resolve these references. File override order and interpolation follow the gotenv parser's rules.

To keep a reference literal, use single quotes or escape the dollar sign:

DOMAIN=example.org
URL="https://${DOMAIN}"           # https://example.org
LITERAL='${DOMAIN}'              # ${DOMAIN}
TEMPLATE="https://\${DOMAIN}"     # https://${DOMAIN}

Values already present in the environment are not expanded again when environment files are loaded. To expand a template explicitly, use container envsubst.

Your shell or Docker Compose may perform interpolation before passing a value to the container. The preservation rule applies to the value received by the container.

docs.title: ⚖️ Positioning and Trade-offs
docs.text:
osixia/baseimage is an opinionated container base image for teams who want more runtime structure than a minimal init, without adopting a full supervision framework.

It is designed to help you build containers faster when you need:

  • predictable lifecycle hooks
  • simple multi-process support
  • operational runtime commands
  • a consistent service layout across images

In practice, it fits well when you do not want to keep rebuilding the same entrypoint logic, service conventions, and debugging workflows in every image.

The trade-off is deliberate: osixia/baseimage is heavier and more opinionated than a minimal PID 1 solution, but it gives you a faster path to reliable application containers.

docs.title: When It Is a Good Fit
docs.text:
osixia/baseimage is usually a good fit if you want to:

  • package one or several tightly related processes in the same image
  • standardize how services start, run, and stop
  • keep image build logic and runtime lifecycle logic clearly separated
  • gain practical runtime tooling for debugging, operations, and CI workflows
  • prototype as a multi-process image first, then split responsibilities later if needed

Typical examples include:

  • application containers with a main process and one or two supporting processes
  • images that need repeatable startup and shutdown behavior
  • teams that want stronger conventions across multiple container images
  • development images that may later be split into more specialized production containers

docs.title: When It Is Probably Not the Right Fit
docs.text:
It is probably not the best choice if you mainly want:

  • the smallest possible image surface
  • a minimal PID 1 with signal forwarding and zombie reaping only
  • a fully generic supervision framework with broader orchestration primitives
  • strict adherence to a one-process-only model with no added runtime conventions

docs.title: Comparison with Alternatives
docs.text: osixia/baseimage sits between a minimal init wrapper and a full supervision framework.

docs.title: Compared with tini
docs.text:
Choose tini if you mainly need a proper PID 1 and want to keep everything else custom.

Choose osixia/baseimage if you also want built-in lifecycle hooks, service conventions, and operational tooling without assembling them yourself.

tini is excellent when you mainly want:

  • a small PID 1
  • signal forwarding
  • zombie reaping

Compared with tini, osixia/baseimage adds:

  • service lifecycle scripts with startup.sh, process.sh, and finish.sh
  • multi-process support
  • service selection with --exec and --skip
  • restart behavior
  • built-in operational commands such as container services, container processes, and container log

Trade-off:

  • tini is smaller and simpler
  • osixia/baseimage is heavier, but gives you much more runtime structure

docs.title: Compared with runit
docs.text:
Choose runit if you want a lightweight supervision toolkit and prefer to define your own conventions.

Choose osixia/baseimage if you want a more Docker-oriented workflow with an opinionated service layout already in place.

runit is a lightweight supervision suite often used to keep several services running in one container.

Compared with runit, osixia/baseimage is generally:

  • easier to approach for Docker users who want a simple image layout
  • more opinionated around service scripts and lifecycle steps
  • more focused on runtime ergonomics than raw supervision primitives

Trade-off:

  • runit is a solid low-level supervisor
  • osixia/baseimage is usually easier when you want a more Docker-oriented workflow and service model

docs.title: Compared with s6-overlay
docs.text:
Choose s6-overlay if you want a more advanced and flexible supervision framework.

Choose osixia/baseimage if you want a simpler operational model with practical conventions for application containers.

s6-overlay is a stronger fit when you want a more general-purpose supervision layer on top of an existing image.

Compared with s6-overlay, osixia/baseimage is generally:

  • easier to adopt for straightforward application containers
  • more opinionated around startup.sh, process.sh, and finish.sh
  • more focused on practical Docker operations and runtime flags

Compared with osixia/baseimage, s6-overlay is generally:

  • more flexible as a supervision system
  • richer for advanced init, service orchestration, and supervision scenarios
  • better suited when you want more of the s6 ecosystem, including its logging model

Trade-off:

  • s6-overlay is more powerful
  • osixia/baseimage is usually simpler to operate

docs.title: Choice Summary
docs.text: If you mainly want... Choose a proper PID 1 with signal forwarding and zombie reaping, and little else tini a small supervision toolkit and the freedom to define your own conventions runit a more advanced and flexible supervision framework s6-overlay an opinionated, application-oriented runtime with simple service conventions and operational tooling osixia/baseimage

docs.title: CI/CD Pipeline Optimization
docs.text:
The project is designed to keep Docker builds cache-friendly.

Recommended pattern:

  1. Download packages and large external resources in Dockerfile RUN layers.
  2. Copy services into /container/services.
  3. Run container services install && container services link.
  4. Copy runtime environment files last.

That is why generated service documentation recommends:

  • keep install.sh for service installation logic only
  • keep heavy downloads outside install.sh when possible
  • use startup.sh for runtime customization based on environment variables

Why this helps:

  • Docker can reuse download layers even if a service script changes.
  • Changing install.sh does not force external dependencies to be downloaded again if those downloads live in earlier Dockerfile layers.
  • Environment files are copied after service installation, so runtime config changes do not invalidate installation layers.

For CI jobs where write durability is not important, --fast-write can also help reduce package install and file operation overhead by disabling fsync and related sync operations through eatmydata. Use it for short-lived build or test containers, not for cases where you need conservative disk-write guarantees.

docs.title: Adding container to an Existing Image
docs.text:
You can also add the container binary to an existing image instead of starting directly from osixia/baseimage.

This is useful when:

  • you already have a working image and want to adopt the lifecycle tooling incrementally
  • you want to keep a custom base image but still use container as entrypoint
  • you want access to commands such as container install, container services, container log, and the managed runtime lifecycle

Example:

FROM debian:trixie-slim

ARG OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_VERSION="2.1.0"
ARG OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_ARCH="amd64"

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y nginx xz-utils
RUN echo "daemon off;" >> /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
CMD ["/usr/sbin/nginx"]

ADD https://github.com/osixia/container-baseimage/releases/download/${OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_VERSION}/container_linux_${OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_ARCH}.tar.gz /tmp
RUN tar -xf /tmp/container_linux_${OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_ARCH}.tar.gz \
    && rm -rf /tmp/* \
    && mv container_linux_${OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_ARCH} /usr/sbin/container \
    && /usr/sbin/container install

ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/sbin/container", "--"]

What this does:

  • installs your application packages as usual
  • downloads a released container binary matching the target architecture
  • installs the baseimage helper files with container install
  • switches the image entrypoint to the osixia runtime wrapper

In practice, once the binary is installed, the image can use the same runtime patterns as an image built directly from osixia/baseimage.

For full entrypoint support, it is better to define a real service with a process.sh script instead of relying only on a plain CMD. That way the image can benefit from the full lifecycle and runtime controls, including:

  • --exec and --skip
  • --restart
  • --step startup|process|finish
  • --pre-startup-cmd, --pre-process-cmd, --pre-finish-cmd, --pre-exit-cmd
  • --bash

Recommended pattern:

FROM debian:trixie-slim

ARG OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_VERSION="2.1.0"
ARG OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_ARCH="amd64"

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y nginx xz-utils

ADD https://github.com/osixia/container-baseimage/releases/download/${OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_VERSION}/container_linux_${OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_ARCH}.tar.gz /tmp
RUN tar -xf /tmp/container_linux_${OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_ARCH}.tar.gz \
    && rm -rf /tmp/* \
    && mv container_linux_${OSIXIA_BASEIMAGE_ARCH} /usr/sbin/container \
    && /usr/sbin/container install

RUN mkdir -p /container/services/nginx

COPY process.sh /container/services/nginx/process.sh

RUN chmod +x /container/services/nginx/process.sh \
    && container services link nginx

ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/sbin/container"]

Example process.sh:

#!/bin/bash -e

container log level eq trace && set -x

exec /usr/sbin/nginx -g "daemon off;" "$@"

Keep in mind:

  • you are responsible for downloading the right binary for your target architecture
  • container install prepares the runtime environment, but your image still needs service files or commands that make sense for your application
  • if you keep a CMD, it becomes the default command executed by container entrypoint
  • if you want the richest integration with the baseimage runtime, prefer service scripts over a bare CMD

docs.title: Container Debugging
docs.text:
Useful runtime options:

  • --bash: starts Bash alongside services or a standalone command
  • --log-level debug|trace
  • --log-format console|json
  • --fast-write: disables fsync via eatmydata for faster ephemeral writes

Useful package-management command:

  • container packages install --debug-tools --update: installs common debugging tools for the current distribution

Useful commands inside a running container:

  • container services status
  • container processes status
  • container processes check <name>: exits with code 1 if a selected process is unexpectedly down
  • container processes stop <name>
  • container processes start <name>
  • container environment print

How debugging works internally:

  • process PID files are stored under /run/container/processes
  • a .down file is used to request a managed process stop
  • stale PID files are cleaned up on startup
  • when the entrypoint is PID 1, it reaps zombie processes and can terminate remaining child processes on exit

Practical debugging examples:

docker run --rm -it my-image --bash --log-level debug

docker run --rm -it my-image --skip-process --bash

docker run --rm my-image --exec nginx --log-level trace

docs.title: Running Read-Only & Rootless Containers
docs.text:
The image supports non-root execution and can work with read-only container filesystems. If you want baseimage runtime process management to work normally, /run/container must be writable.

Why it is needed for process management:

  • runtime state is stored in /run/container
  • process PID files and stop markers are created there, including the state used by container processes
  • the generator also writes there when used inside a container
  • the entrypoint creates /run/container, /run/container/processes, and /run/container/generator with mode 0777 when absent; existing directory permissions are preserved
  • /run/container/tmp provides a shared temporary directory, created with mode 1777 (sticky bit); scripts can use it with mktemp

If your image or runtime flow does not rely on those runtime management features, you may not need /run/container to be writable. But process management and many baseimage features assume it is available.

Typical read-only runtime pattern:

docker run --rm \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /run/container \
  my-image

Typical rootless runtime pattern with the provided non-root image:

docker run --rm \
  --user 65532:65532 \
  my-image

Notes:

  • the repository publishes a dedicated nonroot image target that switches to user nonroot with uid/gid 65532
  • for most non-root use cases, prefer using the provided nonroot image variant directly
  • you can also create your own application user in your Dockerfile if you want explicit uid/gid values or service-specific ownership
  • example:
# Add application group and user
ARG APP_GROUP_GID=10001
ARG APP_USER_UID=10001

RUN container groups add "${APP_GROUP_GID}" app \
    && container users add "${APP_USER_UID}" app --group-id "${APP_GROUP_GID}" --group-name app
  • runtime package installation commands such as container packages install --debug-tools --update generally require enough privileges to use the distribution package manager
  • if the container filesystem is read-only, any service that writes outside writable mounts will still fail

docs.title: Container Logging
docs.text:
Use container log in service scripts when you want messages that follow the container log level and format.

Common commands:

container log info "Starting application"
container log warning "Configuration file is missing"
container log error "Startup failed"
container log debug "Resolved config: ${CONFIG_PATH}"
container log trace "Shell tracing enabled"

container log level can also be used in scripts to inspect the current log level or compare against it.

Show current level:

container log level

Comparison commands:

container log level eq trace
container log level ne info
container log level gt debug
container log level ge debug
container log level lt warning
container log level le info

Those commands exit with status 0 when the comparison is true and 1 otherwise, which makes them convenient in shell scripts.

Typical example:

container log level eq trace && set -x

This enables shell tracing only when the container log level is exactly trace.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Current behavior has a few important constraints:

  • process.sh arguments are shared across all running services; there is no per-service argument mapping
  • multi-process restart is coarse-grained: when restart is enabled, any running process is restarted after it exits, not only on specific exit codes
  • runtime process management expects /run/container to be writable, including container processes state tracking
  • pre-step commands are shell-split, not shell-evaluated; shell features require sh -c or bash -c
  • startup.sh and finish.sh are sequential; only process.sh runs concurrently
  • runtime package installation and debug tooling depend on the underlying distribution package manager and privileges
  • environment files are loaded from /container/environment; existing process environment variables take precedence, including empty values, and are preserved literally without further interpolation

docs.title: Create Your First Image in 2 Minutes
docs.text:
Generate image templates in the osixia-baseimage-example directory

mkdir osixia-baseimage-example
DebianAlpineUbuntu 
docker run --rm --user $UID --volume $(pwd)/osixia-baseimage-example:/run/container/generator \
osixia/baseimage generate bootstrap

docker run --rm --user $UID --volume $(pwd)/osixia-baseimage-example:/run/container/generator \
osixia/baseimage:alpine generate bootstrap

docker run --rm --user $UID --volume $(pwd)/osixia-baseimage-example:/run/container/generator \
osixia/baseimage:ubuntu generate bootstrap

Note: add --multi-process to get a multi-process image sample.

List generated directories and files in osixia-baseimage-example directory 

tree -a osixia-baseimage-example


osixia-baseimage-example
├── Dockerfile
├── environment
│   ├── .env
│   └── README.md
└── services
    └── service-1
        ├── finish.sh
        ├── install.sh
        ├── .priority
        ├── process.sh
        ├── README.md
        └── startup.sh

Take a quick look at the Dockerfile 

FROM osixia/baseimage

ARG IMAGE="osixia/baseimage-example:latest"
ENV CONTAINER_IMAGE=${IMAGE}

# Download services required packages or resources
# RUN container packages install --update --clean \
#        [...]
#     && curl -o resources.tar.gz https://[...].tar.gz \
#     && tar -xzf resources.tar.gz \
#     && rm resources.tar.gz

COPY services /container/services

# Install and link services to the entrypoint
RUN container services install \
    && container services link

COPY environment /container/environment

Build the image example/my-image:develop using files in the osixia-baseimage-example directory 

docker build --tag example/my-image:develop --build-arg IMAGE=example/my-image:develop ./osixia-baseimage-example

Note: --build-arg IMAGE=example/my-image:develop is used to set the image name inside the container.

docker run example/my-image:develop


2026-02-26T11:30:59+01:00 INFO    Container image: example/my-image:develop
2026-02-26T11:30:59+01:00 INFO    Loading environment variables from /container/environment/.env ...
2026-02-26T11:30:59+01:00 INFO    Running /container/services/service-1/startup.sh ...

service-1: EXAMPLE_ENV_VAR=Hello :) ...
2026-02-26T11:30:59+01:00 INFO    Running /container/services/service-1/process.sh ...
service-1: Just going to sleep for 10 seconds ...
2026-02-26T11:31:09+01:00 INFO    Running /container/services/service-1/finish.sh ...

2026-02-26T11:31:09+01:00 INFO    Exiting ...

Detailed documentation regarding the structure, purpose, and usage of the files within the environment and services directories can be found in their respective README.md files.

docs.text:
Single-Process Nginx Image

Multi-Process Nginx + PHP-FPM Image

docs.title: Multi-Process Nginx + PHP-FPM Image
docs.text:
This tutorial extends the nginx tutorial and turns it into a two-service image.

It demonstrates:

  • reusing a previously built image as a base
  • adding a second managed service
  • running Nginx and PHP-FPM as separate processes
  • connecting services through a Unix socket in /run/container
  • packaging both services in one image while still being able to run them in separate containers

docs.title: Prerequisite
docs.text:
This Dockerfile starts from:

FROM osixia/nginx-example

Build the Nginx tutorial first:

docker build -t osixia/nginx-example ../nginx

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
tutorials/nginx-php-fpm/
├── docker-compose.yml
├── Dockerfile
└── services
    └── php-fpm
        ├── .stop-signal
        ├── config
        │   ├── default
        │   └── global.conf
        ├── install.sh
        └── process.sh

These files are available in the container-baseimage repository.

docs.title: Dockerfile
docs.text:
The image:

  • starts from osixia/nginx-example
  • installs the php-fpm package during build
  • copies the php-fpm service into /container/services
  • runs container services install && container services link

It reuses the Nginx service already present in the parent image.

docs.title: services/php-fpm/install.sh
docs.text:
Executed at build time. It:

  • disables expose_php
  • sets cgi.fix_pathinfo=0
  • configures PHP-FPM to listen on /run/container/php-fpm.sock
  • copies config/global.conf into the PHP-FPM pool.d directory
  • configures the socket owner and group as www-data
  • replaces the default Nginx site with the provided PHP-enabled vhost
  • creates /var/www/html/phpinfo.php

This is the integration point between the two services.

docs.title: services/php-fpm/config/default
docs.text:
This Nginx vhost:

  • serves files from /var/www/html
  • keeps standard static file handling
  • forwards *.php requests to unix:/run/container/php-fpm.sock

docs.title: services/php-fpm/process.sh
docs.text:
Executed as the managed PHP-FPM process. It:

  • logs the container IP address and the phpinfo.php URL
  • starts PHP-FPM in the foreground with --nodaemonize
  • forwards any extra entrypoint arguments to PHP-FPM

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
services/php-fpm/.stop-signal contains SIGQUIT. The config/global.conf file sets process_control_timeout = 15s so PHP-FPM gives running requests time to finish.

Keep this application timeout within container --kill-all-timeout (15s by default). The Compose example uses stop_grace_period: 30s for both services, giving the supervisor time to finish before Docker kills the container.

docs.title: docker-compose.yml
docs.text:
This example runs the same multi-process image as two single-purpose containers:

  • nginx runs with --exec nginx
  • php-fpm runs with --exec php-fpm
  • both containers mount the same tmpfs volume on /run/container

This keeps the original Unix socket wiring intact across two containers:

  • PHP-FPM still creates /run/container/php-fpm.sock
  • Nginx still forwards *.php requests to that socket
  • the shared tmpfs keeps socket files and other transient runtime state in memory

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
From this directory:

docker build -t osixia/nginx-php-fpm-example .

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
docker run --rm -p 8080:80 osixia/nginx-php-fpm-example

Then open:

http://localhost:8080/phpinfo.php

Expected runtime behavior:

  • the inherited Nginx service starts
  • the PHP-FPM service starts in parallel
  • Nginx forwards PHP requests to the Unix socket created by PHP-FPM

docs.title: Run as Separate Containers
docs.text:
The image is built as a multi-process image for convenience, but it can still be executed one service at a time.

From the tutorial directory:

docker compose up

This compose setup:

  • uses the same osixia/nginx-php-fpm-example image for both services
  • runs nginx and php-fpm in separate containers with --exec
  • exposes Nginx on http://127.0.0.1:8080
  • mounts the same tmpfs volume on /run/container in both containers
  • keeps the deployment closer to common production layouts

Then open:

http://127.0.0.1:8080/
http://127.0.0.1:8080/phpinfo.php

docs.title: Why Build Multi-Process but Run Separately
docs.text:
This pattern gives you a pragmatic compromise.

Build-time advantages:

  • one image can bundle the full application stack
  • local development and smoke testing stay simple
  • service integration stays close to the code that owns it
  • shared setup logic can live in one place

Runtime advantages:

  • each service gets its own container lifecycle
  • logs are separated by service, which improves observability
  • health checks and restart policies can be tuned per service
  • resource limits can be set independently for Nginx and PHP-FPM
  • scaling becomes more flexible, especially for PHP-FPM workers
  • failures are better isolated
  • debugging is easier because each container has a single main responsibility
  • the topology is closer to what most production platforms expect

Why this compose example keeps the Unix socket:

  • the tutorial image configures PHP-FPM to use /run/container/php-fpm.sock
  • keeping the same socket in Compose makes the multi-container example match the single-container behavior
  • the shared tmpfs volume provides a runtime area both containers can access
  • storing /run/container in tmpfs keeps the shared state ephemeral

docs.title: What This Tutorial Shows
docs.text:
• A multi-process image can be built by layering services across images.
  • .priority does not control process start order; Nginx and PHP-FPM processes are started concurrently.
  • /run/container can be used as a shared runtime area between services.
  • One image can still be split at runtime with service-selection flags.

docs.title: Useful Variants
docs.text:
Run only Nginx:

docker run --rm -p 8080:80 osixia/nginx-php-fpm-example --exec nginx

Run only PHP-FPM:

docker run --rm osixia/nginx-php-fpm-example --exec php-fpm

Debug both services with Bash:

docker run --rm -it -p 8080:80 osixia/nginx-php-fpm-example --bash --log-level debug

To install common debugging tools inside an image based on osixia/baseimage, use:

container packages install --debug-tools --update

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The Nginx service still comes from the parent image, including its startup.sh behavior and .env-driven page customization.
  • The PHP-FPM tutorial does not add an environment/ directory of its own; it relies on what already exists in the parent image.
  • If you run this image with a read-only filesystem, /run/container must still be writable because the PHP-FPM socket is created there.
  • In the compose example, /run/container is backed by a shared tmpfs volume so Nginx and PHP-FPM can keep using the Unix socket across separate containers.

docs.title: Single-Process Nginx Image
docs.text:
This tutorial shows how to build a simple Nginx image on top of osixia/baseimage.

It demonstrates:

  • package installation in the Dockerfile
  • service installation with install.sh
  • runtime customization with startup.sh
  • a foreground web server process managed through process.sh

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
tutorials/nginx
├── Dockerfile
├── environment
└── services
    └── nginx
        ├── .stop-signal
        ├── install.sh
        ├── process.sh
        └── startup.sh

These files are available in the container-baseimage repository.

docs.title: Dockerfile
docs.text:
The image:

  • starts from osixia/baseimage
  • installs the nginx package during build
  • copies the nginx service into /container/services
  • runs container services install && container services link
  • copies environment files into /container/environment

docs.title: environment/.env
docs.text:
Provides:

CUSTOM_MESSAGE="This page is powered by containers, hot chocolate, and questionable YAML decisions."

This value is loaded by the entrypoint before startup.sh runs.

docs.title: services/nginx/install.sh
docs.text:
Executed at build time. It:

  • removes the default Debian Nginx welcome page
  • creates /var/www/html/index.html with the initial content Hi!

Because it runs at build time, it does not depend on runtime environment variables.

docs.title: services/nginx/startup.sh
docs.text:
Executed at container startup before the main process. It:

  • checks for /run/container/nginx-first-start-done
  • appends ${CUSTOM_MESSAGE} to /var/www/html/index.html on first container start only
  • writes the marker file so the message is not appended again while the same container filesystem persists

This is a good example of runtime initialization that depends on environment variables.

docs.title: services/nginx/process.sh
docs.text:
Executed as the managed process. It:

  • logs the container IP address
  • starts Nginx in the foreground with daemon off;
  • forwards any extra entrypoint arguments to Nginx

docs.title: services/nginx/.stop-signal
docs.text: Contains SIGQUIT, so Nginx lets active requests finish during shutdown. The default signal without this file is SIGTERM.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
From this directory:

docker build -t osixia/nginx-example .

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
docker run --rm -p 8080:80 osixia/nginx-example

Then open:

http://localhost:8080

You should see the generated Hi! page with the message from .env appended on first startup.

docs.title: What This Tutorial Shows
docs.text:
• install.sh is used for build-time filesystem preparation.
  • startup.sh is used for runtime customization from environment variables.
  • process.sh contains the long-running foreground command.
  • /run/container is used for runtime state tracking.

docs.title: Useful Variants
docs.text:
Run with debug tools and Bash:

docker run --rm -it -p 8080:80 osixia/nginx-example --bash --log-level debug

To install common debugging tools inside an image based on osixia/baseimage, use:

container packages install --debug-tools --update

Run only the process step:

docker run --rm -p 8080:80 osixia/nginx-example --step process

The second command skips startup.sh, so the custom message from .env is not appended.

docs.title: osixia/keepalived
docs.text: Keepalived container image for VRRP high availability and VIP failover with dynamic configuration and hot reload.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Ready in one command: a virtual IP shared between your nodes, configured with a few environment variables.
  • Three levels of configuration: environment variables, your own template, or your own keepalived.conf.
  • Hot reload: Keepalived reloads when its configuration file changes, without restarting the container.
  • State changes in the container logs: MASTER, BACKUP and FAULT transitions are logged, and you can plug in your own notify script.
  • Up-to-date Keepalived: built from the upstream sources on Alpine, with JSON status support.

docs.title: Start Here
docs.text:
• New to osixia/keepalived? Start with the Quickstart to share a virtual IP between two nodes.
  • Need more than the default setup? See Configuration.
  • Something is not working? Read Troubleshooting.
  • Coming from osixia/keepalived 2.1.5 or older? Read Upgrade.
  • Looking for a setting? All of them are listed in Environment Variables.

This image is based on osixia/baseimage.

On Kubernetes, kube-network-detector can detect which node receives traffic for a VIP and label that node.

docs.title: 🔧 Configuration
docs.text:
There are three ways to configure Keepalived, from the simplest to the most flexible. Pick the first one that covers your needs.

Need Use One VRRP instance, a few VIPs Environment variables Health checks, extra options, still per-node env Your own template Full control Your own keepalived.conf

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The image runs two services:

  • keepalived-conf generates the configuration file at startup, then watches it and reloads Keepalived when it changes.
  • keepalived runs the Keepalived process in the foreground.

The configuration file (KEEPALIVED_CONF, default /etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf) is generated only if it does not exist yet. If you mount your own file, it is used as is.

Environment variables and persisted configuration

Once the file exists, environment variables are no longer applied to it. If /etc/keepalived is on a volume, delete the generated file (or the volume) to regenerate it after changing a variable.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
The default template creates one VRRP instance using unicast:

vrrp_instance VI_1 {
  interface ${KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE}

  state ${KEEPALIVED_STATE}
  virtual_router_id ${KEEPALIVED_ROUTER_ID}
  priority ${KEEPALIVED_PRIORITY}
  nopreempt

  unicast_peer {
    ${KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS}
  }

  virtual_ipaddress {
    ${KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS}
  }

  authentication {
    auth_type PASS
    auth_pass ${KEEPALIVED_PASSWORD}
  }

  notify "${KEEPALIVED_NOTIFY_SCRIPT}"
}

See the Quickstart for a complete example and Environment Variables for the list.

docs.title: Failback
docs.text:
The default template sets nopreempt: a node that comes back does not take the VIP from the current master, even with a higher priority. This avoids a second, useless switch.

nopreempt requires KEEPALIVED_STATE=BACKUP (the default) on every node. The first master is elected by priority. With KEEPALIVED_STATE=MASTER, Keepalived ignores nopreempt and the node takes the VIP back as soon as it returns.

docs.title: Your Own Template
docs.text:
Mount a template and point KEEPALIVED_CONF_TEMPLATE to it. Every ${VARIABLE} is replaced by the matching environment variable, including variables of your own.

This keeps one template for all nodes, with per-node values in the environment.

keepalived.conf.template
vrrp_script check_haproxy {
  script "${CHECK_SCRIPT}"
  interval 2
}

vrrp_instance VI_1 {
  interface ${KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE}
  state BACKUP
  virtual_router_id ${KEEPALIVED_ROUTER_ID}
  priority ${KEEPALIVED_PRIORITY}

  unicast_peer {
    ${KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS}
  }

  virtual_ipaddress {
    ${KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS}
  }

  track_script {
    check_haproxy
  }
}

docker run --detach --name keepalived \
  --network=host --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --cap-add=NET_RAW --cap-add=NET_BROADCAST \
  --volume ./keepalived.conf.template:/etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf.template \
  --env KEEPALIVED_CONF_TEMPLATE="/etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf.template" \
  --env CHECK_SCRIPT="/usr/bin/nc -z 127.0.0.1 443" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE="eth0" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS="192.168.1.231" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS="192.168.1.11" \
  osixia/keepalived

Here the node gives up the VIP when nothing listens on port 443 of the host.

docs.title: Your Own keepalived.conf
docs.text:
Mount your file at KEEPALIVED_CONF. No template is rendered and the KEEPALIVED_* settings of the default template are ignored.

docker run --detach --name keepalived \
  --network=host --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --cap-add=NET_RAW --cap-add=NET_BROADCAST \
  --volume ./keepalived.conf:/etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf \
  osixia/keepalived

docs.title: Hot Reload
docs.text:
When the configuration file changes, Keepalived is reloaded (SIGHUP). The container is not restarted and a master keeps its VIPs if the new configuration still declares them.

echo "# any change" >> ./keepalived.conf

docker logs keepalived
# ... INFO    Change detected on /etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf
# ... INFO    Reloading Keepalived ...
# ... Reload complete

Single-file bind mounts

When you bind-mount a single file, write it in place (cat > keepalived.conf, >>). If an editor replaces it with a new file, Docker keeps the original file mounted inside the container. A manual reload then still reads the old contents.

For editors that save by replacement, mount the containing directory instead. For example, place keepalived.conf in ./keepalived/ and use --volume ./keepalived:/etc/keepalived:ro. The watcher then sees file replacements too.

To run something else on change, set KEEPALIVED_CONF_RELOAD_SCRIPT to your own script.

docs.title: Notify Script
docs.text:
Keepalived calls a notify script on every state change. The default one writes the new state to the container logs:

... INFO    VRRP INSTANCE VI_1 entered MASTER state

To run your own actions (call a webhook, reload a service...), mount a script and set KEEPALIVED_NOTIFY_SCRIPT:

notify.sh
#!/bin/bash

# send the output to the container logs
exec 1>/proc/1/fd/1 2>/proc/1/fd/2

TYPE=$1   # INSTANCE or GROUP
NAME=$2   # VI_1
STATE=$3  # MASTER, BACKUP, FAULT, STOP or DELETED

container log info "VRRP ${TYPE} ${NAME} entered ${STATE} state"

if [ "${STATE}" = "MASTER" ]; then
  wget -q -T 5 -O /dev/null "https://example.org/hook?node=$(hostname)"
fi

chmod +x notify.sh

docker run ... \
  --volume ./notify.sh:/notify.sh \
  --env KEEPALIVED_NOTIFY_SCRIPT="/notify.sh" \
  osixia/keepalived

Set KEEPALIVED_NOTIFY_SCRIPT="" to disable it. With your own keepalived.conf, declare notify yourself.

docs.title: Keepalived Command-Line Arguments
docs.text:
Arguments after -- are passed to the keepalived binary:

docker run ... osixia/keepalived -- --log-detail --dump-conf

List them with:

docker run --rm osixia/keepalived -x keepalived -- --help

docs.title: JSON Status
docs.text:
Keepalived is built with JSON support. Ask the running process to dump its VRRP state:

docker exec keepalived sh -c \
  'kill -s $(keepalived --signum=JSON) $(cat /run/container/processes/keepalived.pid) && sleep 1 && cat /tmp/keepalived.json'

The output contains the state, priority and VIPs of each instance, which makes it easy to feed a monitoring check.

docs.title: Configuration File
docs.text:
Variable Description Default KEEPALIVED_CONF Path to the Keepalived configuration file /etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf KEEPALIVED_CONF_TEMPLATE Path to the configuration template used to generate keepalived.conf /container/services/keepalived-conf/assets/confs/keepalived.conf.template KEEPALIVED_CONF_RELOAD_SCRIPT Script executed when configuration changes are detected /container/services/keepalived-conf/assets/scripts/reload.sh

See Configuration.

docs.title: Default Template
docs.text:
These variables are used by the default template. They are ignored when you mount your own keepalived.conf.

Variable Description Default KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE Network interface used by VRRP, as named on the host eth0 KEEPALIVED_STATE Initial VRRP state (MASTER or BACKUP), see Failback BACKUP KEEPALIVED_ROUTER_ID VRRP router ID (1-255), the same on every node sharing the VIPs 51 KEEPALIVED_PRIORITY VRRP priority of the node (1-254), the highest wins the election 150 KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS Space-separated addresses of the other nodes 192.168.1.10 192.168.1.11 KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS Space-separated virtual IP addresses managed by Keepalived 192.168.1.231 192.168.1.232 KEEPALIVED_PASSWORD VRRP authentication password, the same on every node (8 characters used) d0cker KEEPALIVED_NOTIFY_SCRIPT Script executed when the VRRP state changes, empty to disable /container/services/keepalived/assets/scripts/notify.sh

Warning

Always set KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS, KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS and KEEPALIVED_PASSWORD: the defaults are examples.

docs.title: ⚡ Quickstart
docs.text:
This guide shares one virtual IP (VIP) between two hosts. The VIP is held by one node at a time and moves to the other one when that node goes down.

Host Address Node 1 192.168.1.10 Node 2 192.168.1.11 VIP 192.168.1.231

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• The ip_vs kernel module loaded on each host (modprobe ip_vs).
  • Host networking (--network=host), so Keepalived manages the real interface of the host.
  • The NET_ADMIN, NET_RAW and NET_BROADCAST capabilities.

docs.title: Run Two Nodes
docs.text:
Run one container per host. Only the peer address and the priority change between the two.

Node 1Node 2Docker Compose (node 1) 
docker run --detach --name keepalived \
  --network=host --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --cap-add=NET_RAW --cap-add=NET_BROADCAST \
  --env KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE="eth0" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS="192.168.1.231" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS="192.168.1.11" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_PRIORITY="150" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_PASSWORD="s3cret" \
  osixia/keepalived

docker run --detach --name keepalived \
  --network=host --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --cap-add=NET_RAW --cap-add=NET_BROADCAST \
  --env KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE="eth0" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS="192.168.1.231" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS="192.168.1.10" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_PRIORITY="100" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_PASSWORD="s3cret" \
  osixia/keepalived

services:
  keepalived:
    image: osixia/keepalived
    container_name: keepalived
    network_mode: host
    restart: unless-stopped
    cap_add:
      - NET_ADMIN
      - NET_RAW
      - NET_BROADCAST
    environment:
      KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE: "eth0"
      KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS: "192.168.1.231"
      KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS: "192.168.1.11"
      KEEPALIVED_PRIORITY: "150"
      KEEPALIVED_PASSWORD: "s3cret"

Three things to get right:

  • KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE is the interface name on the host (eth0, ens18, enp2s0...). Check it with ip -br addr.
  • KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS lists the other nodes only, never the node itself.
  • KEEPALIVED_PASSWORD must be the same on every node. VRRP only uses its first 8 characters.

With several values, separate them with spaces: KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS="192.168.1.231 192.168.1.232".

docs.title: Check That It Works
docs.text:
The node with the highest priority takes the VIP:

docker logs keepalived
# ... INFO    VRRP INSTANCE VI_1 entered MASTER state

ip addr show eth0
# inet 192.168.1.10/24 ...
# inet 192.168.1.231/32 scope global eth0

Stop the container on node 1: within a few seconds node 2 logs entered MASTER state and holds the VIP.

Start node 1 again: it comes back as BACKUP and the VIP stays on node 2. This is intended, see Failback.

  • Troubleshooting: debugging options and common issues.
  • Environment Variables: all settings.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
Show more logs, from the image and from Keepalived:

docker run ... osixia/keepalived --log-level debug -- --log-detail --dump-conf

--log-level debug also prints the generated configuration file at startup.

Open a shell next to Keepalived, or without starting it if it keeps crashing:

docker run -it ... osixia/keepalived --log-level debug --bash
docker run -it ... osixia/keepalived --skip-process --log-level debug --bash

List the available options:

docker run --rm osixia/keepalived --help # osixia/baseimage options
docker run --rm osixia/keepalived -x keepalived -- --help # keepalived options

docs.title: Both nodes are MASTER
docs.text:
The nodes do not see each other's VRRP adverts.

  • Allow the VRRP protocol (IP protocol 112) between the nodes in your firewalls.
  • Check that KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS contains the addresses of the other nodes, on the network of KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE.
  • Check that KEEPALIVED_ROUTER_ID and KEEPALIVED_PASSWORD are the same on every node.

docs.title: equal priority advert received from remote host with our IP address
docs.text: The node is listed in its own KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS. Keep only the other nodes.

docs.title: Non-existent interface specified in configuration
docs.text: Keepalived stops and restarts in a loop because KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE does not exist. With --network=host it must be the interface name of the host, rarely eth0. Check it with ip -br addr.

docs.title: Changing an environment variable has no effect
docs.text: The configuration file already exists, so it is not generated again. See How It Works.

docs.title: The configuration is not reloaded after an edit
docs.text: If you bind-mounted a single file, an editor may have replaced the host file while Docker still mounts the old one. Mount the containing directory or write the file in place. See Hot Reload.

docs.title: nopreempt will not work with initial state MASTER
docs.text: Expected with KEEPALIVED_STATE=MASTER. See Failback.

docs.title: The VIP does not come back to the first node
docs.text: Expected with the default template. See Failback.

docs.title: A service cannot bind the VIP on the backup node
docs.text:
The VIP only exists on the master. Bind the service to 0.0.0.0, or allow binding a missing address on the host:

sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind=1

docs.title: The VIP is up but unreachable in a cloud network
docs.text: Many cloud networks drop traffic for addresses they did not assign. The VIP has to be declared to the provider (floating IP, allowed address pairs...), usually from a notify script.

docs.title: From 2.1.5 and Older
docs.text:
Version 2.3.4 moved the image to the new osixia/baseimage. Keepalived itself behaves the same, but the way the container is configured changed. Review the points below before upgrading.

Before Now KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS="#PYTHON2BASH:['192.168.1.10', '192.168.1.11']" KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS="192.168.1.10 192.168.1.11" KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS="#PYTHON2BASH:['192.168.1.231']" KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS="192.168.1.231" KEEPALIVED_NOTIFY KEEPALIVED_NOTIFY_SCRIPT KEEPALIVED_COMMAND_LINE_ARGUMENTS="--log-detail" docker run ... osixia/keepalived -- --log-detail Config mounted at /container/service/keepalived/assets/keepalived.conf Config mounted at /etc/keepalived/keepalived.conf Template placeholders {{ KEEPALIVED_PRIORITY }} Template placeholders ${KEEPALIVED_PRIORITY} YAML files in /container/environment/01-custom/ Plain environment variables (--env, --env-file)

Other changes:

  • --log-detail --dump-conf are no longer passed to Keepalived by default. Add them after -- if you rely on them.
  • A mounted keepalived.conf is used as is: placeholders are only replaced in a template, see Your Own Template.
  • The default notify script moved to /container/services/keepalived/assets/scripts/notify.sh.
  • The image name is unchanged (osixia/keepalived). The GitHub repository is now osixia/container-keepalived.

docs.text:
BeforeNow 
docker run --detach \
  --network=host --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --cap-add=NET_RAW --cap-add=NET_BROADCAST \
  --env KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE="eth0" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS="#PYTHON2BASH:['192.168.1.10', '192.168.1.11']" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS="#PYTHON2BASH:['192.168.1.231']" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_COMMAND_LINE_ARGUMENTS="--log-detail" \
  osixia/keepalived:2.1.5

docker run --detach \
  --network=host --cap-add=NET_ADMIN --cap-add=NET_RAW --cap-add=NET_BROADCAST \
  --env KEEPALIVED_INTERFACE="eth0" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_UNICAST_PEERS="192.168.1.11" \
  --env KEEPALIVED_VIRTUAL_IPS="192.168.1.231" \
  osixia/keepalived:2.4.3 -- --log-detail

Upgrade the backup node first, check its logs, then upgrade the master.

docs.title: Between 2.x Versions
docs.text: Change the image tag and recreate the container, one node at a time. Image changes are listed in the changelog, Keepalived changes in the upstream release notes.

docs.title: osixia/openldap
docs.text:
OpenLDAP container image with built-in bootstrap, backup helpers, TLS, replication and upgrade support.

110M+ pulls 🎉 Thanks to everyone using, testing, reporting issues, and contributing to this image. 🙏

v2 is a breaking release

Existing v1 deployments are not migrated automatically and require a manual migration to move to v2. Automatic upgrade paths are intended only between v2 versions (for example, v2.x to v2.y). See Upgrade.

docs.title: 🛟 Backup / Restore
docs.text: The image includes the openldap-ctl helper with backup and restore commands. Backups are gzip-compressed LDIF exports of the configuration and data databases.

docs.title: Create a Backup
docs.text:
docker exec openldap container run -- openldap-ctl backup my-backup

This creates two files in /var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups (OPENLDAP_BACKUP_DIR):

  • my-backup-config.gz
  • my-backup-data.gz

Backups can be taken while OpenLDAP is running.

Usage:

openldap-ctl backup file-prefix [--config] [--data] [--clean days] [--clean-prefix prefix]
Option Description --config Back up only the configuration database --data Back up only the data database --clean days After the backup, delete backup files older than days days --clean-prefix prefix Limit cleanup to backup filenames starting with this prefix; requires --clean

Without --config or --data, both databases are backed up.

Create a data backup and remove only daily- backups older than 15 days:

docker exec openldap container run -- \
  openldap-ctl backup "daily-$(date -I)" --data --clean 15 --clean-prefix daily-

Warning

Without --clean-prefix, cleanup applies to all old files ending in -config.gz or -data.gz in the backup directory, including manual and upgrade backups. A data-only backup can also clean configuration backups. Always set a prefix when you want to preserve other backup sets.

docs.title: Restore a Backup
docs.text:
docker exec openldap container run -- openldap-ctl restore my-backup --force

Usage:

openldap-ctl restore file-prefix [--config] [--data] [--force]
Option Description --config Restore only the configuration database --data Restore only the data database --force Stop OpenLDAP if running and replace the selected databases

A restore goes through these steps:

  1. The backup files are checked. If one is missing or is not a valid gzip archive, the command stops and nothing is changed.
  2. If OpenLDAP is running, it is stopped. This requires --force.
  3. The selected databases are moved into .restore-previous directories. Replacing existing data requires --force.
  4. The selected databases are restored, and the data database is re-indexed.
  5. On success, the previous data is removed. On failure, the command attempts to put it back. OpenLDAP is started again if it was running.

If a restore is interrupted and leaves a .restore-previous directory, the next restore refuses to proceed. Inspect the files and recover the previous data before trying again.

Without --force, the command refuses to run when OpenLDAP is running or when the target directories are not empty.

Danger

--force deletes the current configuration and data. Take a backup first if you may need them.

docs.title: Scheduled Backups
docs.text:
The openldap-cron service runs backups on a schedule. It is disabled by default and is meant to run in a separate container that shares the configuration, data and backup volumes:

docker run --name openldap-cron \
  -u root \
  -v openldap-conf:/etc/openldap/slapd.d \
  -v openldap-data:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-data \
  -v openldap-backups:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc -x openldap-cron

The container must run as root for crond; the backup itself runs as the ldap user.

The schedule and command are defined by OPENLDAP_CRON_JOB. By default, a full backup runs every day at 02:15 and only scheduled backups older than 15 days are deleted:

15 2 * * * PATH=${PATH} container run -- openldap-ctl backup "openldap-cron-$(date -I)-${OPENLDAP_VERSION}" --clean 15 --clean-prefix openldap-cron-

This produces files such as openldap-cron-2026-10-13-2.6.15-r0-config.gz and preserves manual and upgrade backups.

docs.title: Keeping Backups Safe
docs.text:
Backups contain password hashes, and the configuration backup also contains the replication password when replication is enabled. Files are created readable by the ldap user only.

Copy backups out of the backup volume to another machine or storage: a backup stored next to the data it protects does not survive the loss of the host.
