docs.title: 🧩 How It Works
docs.text: osixia/openldap is built on osixia/baseimage. The image is split into small services, each with its own startup script. Understanding which service does what makes the rest of this documentation easier to follow.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
Service Enabled by default Role openldap yes Checks directories, copies custom modules and schemas, then runs slapd openldap-bootstrap yes Creates the configuration and data on first start openldap-upgrade yes Records the OpenLDAP version and migrates the databases when the image version changes openldap-pre-upgrade no Backs up the databases before an upgrade; meant to run as an init container openldap-cron no Runs scheduled backups; meant to run in a separate container openldap-tls-reload no Watches certificate files and restarts OpenLDAP when their contents change

Optional services are started explicitly with the baseimage -x (--exec) flag, for example osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc -x openldap-cron. See Backup / Restore, Upgrade and TLS.

docs.title: Startup Sequence
docs.text:
Startup scripts run in priority order before slapd is started:

  1. openldap checks that the configuration and data directories exist, then copies custom modules and schemas into the OpenLDAP directories.
  2. openldap-bootstrap creates a new directory if both the configuration and data directories are empty. Otherwise it does nothing.
  3. openldap-upgrade compares the image version with the version recorded in the configuration directory and migrates the databases if needed.
  4. slapd starts in the foreground.

docs.title: Bootstrap Runs Once
docs.text:
Bootstrap only runs when both /etc/openldap/slapd.d and /var/lib/openldap/openldap-data are empty. Hidden files and lost+found are ignored.

This has two consequences:

  • OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_* variables are only read on first start. Changing them later has no effect on an existing directory.
  • After bootstrap, the directory is managed like any OpenLDAP server: change the configuration through cn=config with ldapmodify.

See Bootstrap for what is created and how to customize it.

docs.title: Directories
docs.text:
Path Variable Content /etc/openldap/slapd.d OPENLDAP_CONF_DIR Configuration database (cn=config) /var/lib/openldap/openldap-data OPENLDAP_DATA_DIR Data database (MDB) /var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups OPENLDAP_BACKUP_DIR Backups /etc/openldap/schema OPENLDAP_SCHEMAS_DIR Schemas available to bootstrap /usr/lib/openldap OPENLDAP_MODULES_DIR OpenLDAP modules /container/services/openldap/assets/schema OPENLDAP_CUSTOM_SCHEMAS_DIR Custom schemas copied at startup /container/services/openldap/assets/module OPENLDAP_CUSTOM_MODULES_DIR Custom modules copied at startup /container/services/openldap/assets/certs Default location of TLS certificates

The first three should be persisted with volumes.

docs.title: User and Ports
docs.text:
• The container runs as the ldap user (uid 911, gid 911), not as root.
  • slapd listens on ldap://:3890, ldaps://:6360 and the local ldapi:/// socket, as defined by OPENLDAP_URLS. Unprivileged ports are used because the process is not root; publish them on 389 and 636 if needed.
  • The local ldapi:/// socket gives the ldap user full access to the data and monitor databases. This is what docker exec openldap container run -- ldapsearch -Q -Y EXTERNAL -H ldapi:/// ... uses.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
Defaults are stored in .env files inside the image and loaded at startup. Variables passed to the container take precedence, and defaults that reference other variables follow them: setting OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX also changes OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_ROOT_DN, which defaults to cn=admin,${OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX}.

See Environment Variables for the full list.

docs.title: 🛠️ LDAP Toolkit
docs.text:
The image ships with the full suite of OpenLDAP utilities and with openldap-ctl, a helper for common tasks. They can be used inside a running container or in a throwaway one.

docker exec openldap container run -- <command>   # inside a running container
docker run --rm osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- <command>  # in a throwaway container

container run -- loads the image environment variables before running the command.

docs.title: Database Tools
docs.text:
slapcat, slapadd, slapindex and slaptest operate directly on the local database files and must run inside the container.

Export the data database to LDIF:

docker exec openldap container run -- slapcat -n 1

Export the configuration database (cn=config):

docker exec openldap container run -- slapcat -n 0

Note

slapadd and slapindex require OpenLDAP to be stopped first:

docker exec openldap container processes stop openldap
docker exec openldap container processes start openldap

For a full export and import, prefer openldap-ctl backup and restore.

docs.title: LDAP Client Tools
docs.text:
ldapsearch, ldapwhoami, ldapadd, ldapmodify, ldapdelete and ldappasswd connect to any LDAP server over the network.

Search for all entries under a base DN:

docker run --rm osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- \
  ldapsearch -H ldap://172.16.0.1 \
  -D "cn=admin,dc=example,dc=org" -w passw0rd \
  -b "dc=example,dc=org" "(objectClass=*)"

Verify bind credentials:

docker run --rm osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- \
  ldapwhoami -H ldap://172.16.0.1 \
  -D "cn=admin,dc=example,dc=org" -w passw0rd

Add entries from a local LDIF file:

docker run --rm -v /path/to/entries.ldif:/tmp/entries.ldif \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- \
  ldapadd -H ldap://172.16.0.1 \
  -D "cn=admin,dc=example,dc=org" -w passw0rd \
  -f /tmp/entries.ldif

Change a user's password:

docker run --rm osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- \
  ldappasswd -H ldap://172.16.0.1 \
  -D "cn=admin,dc=example,dc=org" -w passw0rd \
  -s newpassword "uid=jdoe,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"

docs.title: Local Administration Without a Password
docs.text:
Inside the container, the ldap user has full access to the data database through the local socket:

docker exec openldap container run -- \
  ldapsearch -Q -Y EXTERNAL -H ldapi:/// -b "dc=example,dc=org"

To pipe an LDIF file from the host, add -i to docker exec:

docker exec -i openldap container run -- \
  ldapadd -Q -Y EXTERNAL -H ldapi:/// < entries.ldif

docs.title: openldap-ctl
docs.text:
docker run --rm osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- openldap-ctl --help
Command Description backup Back up the configuration and data databases restore Restore a backup validate-ldif Check data LDIF against the initialized configuration without importing it password Generate or hash a password schema2ldif Convert a .schema file to cn=config LDIF

backup and restore are described in Backup / Restore.

docs.title: Validate LDIF
docs.text:
Check entries against the instance's schemas without importing them or stopping OpenLDAP. First copy the file into the running container:

docker cp users.ldif openldap:/tmp/users.ldif
docker exec openldap container run -- openldap-ctl validate-ldif /tmp/users.ldif

You can pass several files or a directory. Directories are searched recursively for *.ldif, excluding hidden paths. Each file must contain complete data entries. The command checks syntax, attribute values and schemas, and returns a non-zero status if validation fails.

It requires initialized OpenLDAP configuration. It does not check existing entries, ACLs or overlay rules, and does not accept ldapmodify change records.

docs.title: Password Helpers
docs.text:
Generate a random password:

docker run --rm osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- openldap-ctl password generate

Hash a password:

docker run --rm osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- openldap-ctl password hash 'passw0rd'

The result is an Argon2 hash, ready to be used in a *_PASSWORD_HASHED bootstrap variable or in a userPassword attribute:

{ARGON2}$argon2id$v=19$m=7168,t=5,p=1$...

Quote the password with single quotes so the shell does not interpret special characters.

To read a password from a file or standard input:

docker run --rm --user "$UID" -v "$PWD/password.txt:/run/secrets/password:ro" \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- openldap-ctl password hash --file /run/secrets/password
docker run --rm -i osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- \
  openldap-ctl password hash --stdin < password.txt

The contents are hashed exactly, including trailing newlines. Use hash -- password for a literal password named --file, --stdin or --.

Both commands can be changed with OPENLDAP_CTL_PASSWORD_GENERATE_CMD and OPENLDAP_CTL_PASSWORD_HASH_CMD.

docs.title: Convert Schema to LDIF
docs.text:
OpenLDAP loads schemas in cn=config LDIF format. schema2ldif converts a traditional .schema file:

docker run --rm --user $UID -v $(pwd)/schema:/data \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- openldap-ctl schema2ldif /data/test.schema

The LDIF file is written next to the source file, here schema/test.ldif, and printed. The command fails if the LDIF file already exists.

Usage:

openldap-ctl schema2ldif "schema-files" ["dependencies"]
  • Several schema files can be converted at once, separated by spaces in a single quoted argument.
  • Schemas the converted file depends on are listed in the second argument. The default is core.schema cosine.schema inetorgperson.schema (OPENLDAP_CTL_SCHEMA2LDIF_DEPENDENCIES).

To load the result at bootstrap, see Schemas.

docs.title: Run a First Server
docs.text:
Run a basic OpenLDAP server:

docker run --name openldap --hostname ldap.example.org -p 389:3890 -p 636:6360 \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_ORGANIZATION="Keycloakers Org" \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX="dc=keycloakers,dc=org" \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

On first start the container bootstraps a new directory: it creates the configuration, the database for the suffix and the root entry, then starts slapd.

Notes:

  • The container listens on ports 3890 (LDAP) and 6360 (LDAPS), as defined by OPENLDAP_URLS.
  • OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX must start with dc= (for example dc=example,dc=org).
  • Passwords are generated when no hashed value is provided and are printed in the logs, once.
  • Bootstrap runs only when the configuration and data directories are empty.

docs.title: Keep Your Data
docs.text:
For persistent deployments, mount the configuration, data and backup directories:

DockerDocker Compose 
docker run --name openldap --hostname ldap.example.org -p 389:3890 -p 636:6360 \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_ORGANIZATION="Keycloakers Org" \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX="dc=keycloakers,dc=org" \
  -v openldap-conf:/etc/openldap/slapd.d \
  -v openldap-data:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-data \
  -v openldap-backups:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

services:
  openldap:
    image: osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc
    container_name: openldap
    ports:
      - "389:3890"
      - "636:6360"
    environment:
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_ORGANIZATION: "Keycloakers Org"
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX: "dc=keycloakers,dc=org"
    volumes:
      - openldap-conf:/etc/openldap/slapd.d
      - openldap-data:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-data
      - openldap-backups:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups

volumes:
  openldap-conf:
  openldap-data:
  openldap-backups:
Path Content /etc/openldap/slapd.d OpenLDAP configuration (cn=config) /var/lib/openldap/openldap-data Directory data (MDB database) /var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups Backups created by openldap-ctl backup

The container runs as the ldap user (uid 911, gid 911). Bind-mounted host directories must be writable by that user.

docs.title: Verify the Server Is Up
docs.text:
Retrieve the generated passwords from the container logs:

docker logs openldap 2>&1 | grep -i password

Then search the base DN to confirm the server is responding, replacing <database root password> with the password from the logs:

docker exec openldap container run -- \
  ldapsearch -H ldap://localhost:3890 \
  -D "cn=admin,dc=keycloakers,dc=org" -w '<database root password>' \
  -b "dc=keycloakers,dc=org" "(objectClass=*)"

A successful response returns the organization entry.

Set your own passwords

To choose the passwords instead of reading generated ones from the logs, hash them with openldap-ctl password hash and pass the result in OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_ROOT_PASSWORD_HASHED and OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_ROOT_PASSWORD_HASHED. See LDAP Toolkit.

docs.title: Passing Command-Line Arguments to OpenLDAP
docs.text:
Arguments specified after -- are forwarded to the slapd process inside the container:

docker run osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc -- -d -1

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
To debug the container manually, you can start it with an interactive shell.

The --log-level debug --bash options from osixia/baseimage enable debug logging and launch an interactive shell.

If OpenLDAP keeps crashing, add --skip-process to start the container without launching service processes.

docker run -it osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc --log-level debug --bash
docker run -it osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc --skip-process --log-level debug --bash

You can also increase the slapd log level with OPENLDAP_DEBUG_LEVEL:

docker run -e OPENLDAP_DEBUG_LEVEL=-1 osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

Note

OPENLDAP_DEBUG_LEVEL only affects slapd logging. To increase container logs, use the baseimage flag --log-level (for example --log-level debug). Bootstrap errors reported by slapadd are logged at the debug level.

To see all available command-line options:

docker run --rm osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc --help # osixia/baseimage options
docker run --rm osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc -x openldap -- --help # slapd command-line options

docs.title: 🔁 Replication
docs.text: Set OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION=true to bootstrap multi-provider replication: every server accepts writes and replicates the data database to the others with syncrepl.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_HOSTS lists two to nine servers, in the same order on every server.
  • The container hostname (FQDN) must match one of the hosts in that list.
  • OPENLDAP_URLS must use the same host name as the list, so that each server recognizes its own URL.
  • The replication password must be the same on every server. Set OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_DATA_READONLY_PASSWORD explicitly: if it is empty, each server generates a different one and replication fails.
  • All servers must be bootstrapped with the same suffix and the same schemas.

docs.title: Two-Node Example
docs.text:
DockerDocker Compose

Put both containers on the same user-defined network so each host can resolve the other one:

docker network create openldap-net

First server, ldap1.example.org:

docker run --name ldap1 --network openldap-net --hostname ldap1.example.org \
  -e OPENLDAP_URLS="ldap://ldap1.example.org:3890 ldaps://ldap1.example.org:6360 ldapi:///" \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_ORGANIZATION="Keycloakers Org" \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX="dc=keycloakers,dc=org" \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION=true \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_HOSTS="ldap://ldap1.example.org:3890 ldap://ldap2.example.org:3890" \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_DATA_READONLY_PASSWORD="passw0rd" \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

Second server, ldap2.example.org:

docker run --name ldap2 --network openldap-net --hostname ldap2.example.org \
  -e OPENLDAP_URLS="ldap://ldap2.example.org:3890 ldaps://ldap2.example.org:6360 ldapi:///" \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_ORGANIZATION="Keycloakers Org" \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX="dc=keycloakers,dc=org" \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION=true \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_HOSTS="ldap://ldap1.example.org:3890 ldap://ldap2.example.org:3890" \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_DATA_READONLY_PASSWORD="passw0rd" \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

services:
  ldap1:
    image: osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc
    container_name: ldap1
    hostname: ldap1.example.org
    networks:
      - openldap-net
    ports:
      - "389:3890"
      - "636:6360"
    environment:
      OPENLDAP_URLS: "ldap://ldap1.example.org:3890 ldaps://ldap1.example.org:6360 ldapi:///"
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_ORGANIZATION: "Keycloakers Org"
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX: "dc=keycloakers,dc=org"
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION: "true"
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_HOSTS: "ldap://ldap1.example.org:3890 ldap://ldap2.example.org:3890"
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_DATA_READONLY_PASSWORD: "passw0rd"
    volumes:
      - ldap1-conf:/etc/openldap/slapd.d
      - ldap1-data:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-data
      - ldap1-backups:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups

  ldap2:
    image: osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc
    container_name: ldap2
    hostname: ldap2.example.org
    networks:
      - openldap-net
    environment:
      OPENLDAP_URLS: "ldap://ldap2.example.org:3890 ldaps://ldap2.example.org:6360 ldapi:///"
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_ORGANIZATION: "Keycloakers Org"
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX: "dc=keycloakers,dc=org"
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION: "true"
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_HOSTS: "ldap://ldap1.example.org:3890 ldap://ldap2.example.org:3890"
      OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_DATA_READONLY_PASSWORD: "passw0rd"
    volumes:
      - ldap2-conf:/etc/openldap/slapd.d
      - ldap2-data:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-data
      - ldap2-backups:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups

networks:
  openldap-net:

volumes:
  ldap1-conf:
  ldap1-data:
  ldap1-backups:
  ldap2-conf:
  ldap2-data:
  ldap2-backups:

An entry added on one server then appears on the other.

Passwords

Only the replication password is shared through this example. Root passwords are generated separately on each server unless you set OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_ROOT_PASSWORD_HASHED and OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_ROOT_PASSWORD_HASHED to the same values on all of them. Once replication is running, the data database content is the same everywhere.

docs.title: What Bootstrap Configures
docs.text:
• A server ID for each host, in list order (olcServerID).
  • A replication account, cn=replicator,<suffix>, that can read the whole data database, with no size or time limit.
  • One olcSyncRepl consumer per other server, in refreshAndPersist mode.
  • Multi-provider mode on the data database (olcMultiProvider: TRUE).
  • The syncprov overlay, loaded last.

Only the data database is replicated. The configuration database (cn=config) is not: apply configuration changes on each server.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
Replication uses StartTLS when OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_TLS=true. It defaults to the value of OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_REQUIRED, so replication is encrypted as soon as TLS is required.

Each server then verifies the certificate of the others (starttls=critical tls_reqcert=demand): certificates must match the host names in OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_HOSTS and be signed by the configured CA.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Variable Description Default OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_HOSTS Servers list; two to nine, same order on every server ldap://ldap1.example.org:3890 ldap://ldap2.example.org:3890 OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_DATA_READONLY_DN Replication account DN cn=replicator,${OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX} OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_DATA_READONLY_PASSWORD Plain replication password; generated if empty empty OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_SYNCPROV_CHECKPOINT syncprov checkpoint 100 10 OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_TLS Use StartTLS for replication ${OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_REQUIRED} OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_MEMBEROF Exclude memberOf from replication ${OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MEMBEROF}

The generated olcSyncRepl value can be changed with OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_DATA_SYNC_REPL_TEMPLATE. See Environment Variables.

Note

The replication password is stored in plain text in the olcSyncRepl configuration, as OpenLDAP requires. The configuration database is only readable by its root DN.

docs.title: Changing the Topology
docs.text: Replication is configured at bootstrap only. Adding or removing a server later means updating olcServerID and olcSyncRepl on every existing server with ldapmodify, then bootstrapping the new server with the full host list.

docs.title: 🔐 TLS
docs.text: TLS is configured at bootstrap. Set OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS=true and provide a certificate, its private key and the CA certificate.

docs.title: Enable TLS
docs.text:
The default certificate paths are:

  • /container/services/openldap/assets/certs/tls.crt
  • /container/services/openldap/assets/certs/tls.key
  • /container/services/openldap/assets/certs/ca.crt

The simplest way is to mount a directory that contains files with exactly those names:

docker run --name openldap --hostname ldap.example.org -p 389:3890 -p 636:6360 \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS=true \
  -v $PWD/certs:/container/services/openldap/assets/certs \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

The files must be readable by the ldap user (uid 911).

Once TLS is enabled, clients can connect with:

  • LDAPS on port 6360 (ldaps://);
  • StartTLS on port 3890 (ldap://).

The certificate must match the name clients use to reach the server, here ldap.example.org.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Variable Description Default OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_CERT Server certificate path /container/services/openldap/assets/certs/tls.crt OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_CERT_KEY Server private key path /container/services/openldap/assets/certs/tls.key OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_CA_CERT CA certificate path /container/services/openldap/assets/certs/ca.crt OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_VERIFY_CLIENT Value for olcTLSVerifyClient allow OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_PROTOCOL_MIN Value for olcTLSProtocolMin 3.4
  • OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_PROTOCOL_MIN=3.4 means TLS 1.3 is the minimum version. Use 3.3 to also accept TLS 1.2.
  • OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_VERIFY_CLIENT=allow means a client certificate is requested but not required. Use demand to require a valid client certificate, or never to not request one.

docs.title: Require TLS
docs.text:
By default, enabling TLS does not forbid unencrypted connections on port 3890.

Set OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_REQUIRED=true to reject them:

docker run --name openldap --hostname ldap.example.org -p 389:3890 -p 636:6360 \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS=true \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_REQUIRED=true \
  -v $PWD/certs:/container/services/openldap/assets/certs \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

Bootstrap then requires a security strength of at least 128 bits for every operation (olcSecurity: ssf=128). The local ldapi:/// socket is treated as secure, so administration from inside the container keeps working.

When TLS is required, replication uses StartTLS by default.

Warning

OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_REQUIRED=true without OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS=true makes the server unreachable over the network. Bootstrap logs a warning in that case.

docs.title: Renewing Certificates
docs.text:
Certificate paths are stored in the configuration at bootstrap. To renew a certificate, replace the files at the same paths and restart the container.

For automatic renewal handling, run the optional openldap-tls-reload service alongside the normal services. Add these arguments after the image name in your docker run command:

--exec openldap --exec openldap-bootstrap --exec openldap-upgrade --exec openldap-tls-reload

The watcher compares certificate contents and restarts the OpenLDAP process when they change. The container stays running, but LDAP connections can be interrupted briefly.

With the Helm chart, set openldap.tlsReload.enabled=true to run the watcher as a sidecar. Keep the certificate volume mounted as a directory so Kubernetes Secret updates remain visible.

To change TLS settings on an existing directory, modify the olcTLS* attributes of cn=config with ldapmodify.

docs.title: ⏫ Upgrade
docs.text:
OpenLDAP database files are not guaranteed to be readable by a newer OpenLDAP release. The safe way to upgrade is to export the databases with the old version and import them with the new one.

The image automates this with two services:

  • openldap-pre-upgrade exports the databases. It runs with the previous image version, as an init container.
  • openldap-upgrade imports them. It runs with the new image version, in the main container, before slapd starts.

docs.title: The Principle
docs.text:
Always run two containers on the same volumes, one version apart:

Container Image version Command Init container n-1 -x openldap -x openldap-pre-upgrade --skip-process Main container n default

To upgrade, increment both versions: the init container moves to n, the main container to n+1.

On each start:

  1. The init container compares its own version with the version recorded in the configuration directory. If they match, the directory has not been migrated yet: it backs up both databases, then exits.
  2. The main container compares its version with the recorded one. If they differ, it restores the backup made by the init container, then records its own version.
  3. slapd starts.

On following starts, the recorded version already matches the main container: the init container does nothing, and neither does the upgrade service.

Because the backup is taken by the init container right before the main container starts, with slapd stopped, nothing is lost between the export and the import.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Replace <previous-version> and <new-version> with image tags. The three volumes must be shared by both containers.

Docker ComposeKubernetesDocker 
services:
  openldap-pre-upgrade:
    image: osixia/openldap:<previous-version>
    command: ["-x", "openldap", "-x", "openldap-pre-upgrade", "--skip-process"]
    volumes:
      - openldap-conf:/etc/openldap/slapd.d
      - openldap-data:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-data
      - openldap-backups:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups

  openldap:
    image: osixia/openldap:<new-version>
    depends_on:
      openldap-pre-upgrade:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    ports:
      - "389:3890"
      - "636:6360"
    volumes:
      - openldap-conf:/etc/openldap/slapd.d
      - openldap-data:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-data
      - openldap-backups:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups

volumes:
  openldap-conf:
  openldap-data:
  openldap-backups:

spec:
  securityContext:
    fsGroup: 911
  initContainers:
    - name: openldap-pre-upgrade
      image: osixia/openldap:<previous-version>
      args: ["-x", "openldap", "-x", "openldap-pre-upgrade", "--skip-process"]
      volumeMounts:
        - { name: conf, mountPath: /etc/openldap/slapd.d }
        - { name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/openldap/openldap-data }
        - { name: backups, mountPath: /var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups }
  containers:
    - name: openldap
      image: osixia/openldap:<new-version>
      ports:
        - { name: ldap, containerPort: 3890 }
        - { name: ldaps, containerPort: 6360 }
      volumeMounts:
        - { name: conf, mountPath: /etc/openldap/slapd.d }
        - { name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/openldap/openldap-data }
        - { name: backups, mountPath: /var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups }

docker stop openldap && docker rm openldap

docker run --rm \
  -v openldap-conf:/etc/openldap/slapd.d \
  -v openldap-data:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-data \
  -v openldap-backups:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups \
  osixia/openldap:<previous-version> -x openldap -x openldap-pre-upgrade --skip-process

docker run --name openldap -p 389:3890 -p 636:6360 \
  -v openldap-conf:/etc/openldap/slapd.d \
  -v openldap-data:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-data \
  -v openldap-backups:/var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups \
  osixia/openldap:<new-version>

If the backup fails, the init container exits with an error and the main container does not start.

Selecting openldap with --skip-process prepares custom modules and schemas before the backup, without starting slapd. Mount the same custom resources in both containers when you use them.

docs.title: Migration Level
docs.text:
OPENLDAP_UPGRADE_MIGRATION_LEVEL defines which version change triggers a migration:

Level A migration runs when… Example major the major version changes 2.x → 3.x minor (default) the major or minor version changes 2.6.x → 2.7.x patch any version number changes 2.6.10 → 2.6.15

With the default level, moving from 2.6.10 to 2.6.15 does not migrate anything: the new image starts directly on the existing files.

Use the same level in the init container and in the main container.

Note

While both containers are within the same level, for example 2.6.10 and 2.6.15 at the minor level, the init container takes a backup on every start. It is overwritten each time.

docs.title: What You See in the Logs
docs.text:
A migration from 2.6 to 2.7:

INFO    Migration level set to 'minor'
INFO    OpenLDAP version: 2.7.0-r0, conf version: 2.6.10-r0
WARNING Migration required: 2.6 → 2.7
WARNING Deleting data in /etc/openldap/slapd.d ...
INFO    Restoring OpenLDAP config ...
WARNING Deleting data in /var/lib/openldap/openldap-data ...
INFO    Restoring OpenLDAP data ...
INFO    Writing OpenLDAP version 2.7.0-r0 to /etc/openldap/slapd.d/.version ...

A normal start:

INFO    OpenLDAP version: 2.7.0-r0, conf version: 2.7.0-r0
INFO    No migration needed at minor level

docs.title: Safeguards
docs.text:
The upgrade service refuses to continue in two cases. In both, the container stops before slapd starts and nothing is changed.

The backup is missing. The main container needs a migration but the init container did not run:

ERROR   Missing /var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups/openldap-upgrade-2.7-config.gz or
        /var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups/openldap-upgrade-2.7-data.gz.
        Set OPENLDAP_UPGRADE_FORCE=true to bypass.

Run the init container with the previous image version, then start the main container again.

The new version is older than the recorded one. Downgrades are refused:

ERROR   Downgrade forbidden: 2.7 → 2.6. Set OPENLDAP_UPGRADE_FORCE=true to bypass.

docs.title: Forcing
docs.text:
OPENLDAP_UPGRADE_FORCE=true bypasses both safeguards:

  • a downgrade is no longer refused;
  • when the backup is missing, the migration is skipped and slapd starts on the existing files. The recorded version is not updated, so the warning is logged on every start until a migration actually runs.

Danger

Forcing means running a version of OpenLDAP on database files written by another one. Take a backup first and keep it outside the volumes.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
File Content /etc/openldap/slapd.d/.version OpenLDAP version of the last migration /var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups/openldap-upgrade-<version>-config.gz Configuration backup taken by the init container /var/lib/openldap/openldap-backups/openldap-upgrade-<version>-data.gz Data backup taken by the init container

<version> is the recorded version truncated to the migration level, for example 2.6 at the minor level. Upgrade backups are kept after the migration; remove them when you no longer need them.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Variable Description Default OPENLDAP_UPGRADE_MIGRATION_LEVEL Version change that triggers a migration minor OPENLDAP_UPGRADE_FORCE Bypass the missing-backup and downgrade safeguards false OPENLDAP_UPGRADE_BACKUP_FILES_PREFIX Prefix of upgrade backup files openldap-upgrade OPENLDAP_UPGRADE_CONF_VERSION_FILE File storing the recorded version ${OPENLDAP_CONF_DIR}/.version

docs.title: Replicated Servers
docs.text: Upgrade one server at a time, each with its own init container, and wait for it to be back and in sync before upgrading the next one.

docs.title: Migrating From v1
docs.text:
v2 is a complete rewrite and v1 deployments are not migrated automatically. The procedure above only applies between v2 versions.

To move from v1 to v2, export the data from the v1 server as LDIF, start a new v2 server with the same suffix, then import the entries. Configuration (cn=config) is not portable as is: recreate it with bootstrap settings and custom LDIF.

docs.title: 🚀 Bootstrap
docs.text:
On first start, the openldap-bootstrap service creates a complete directory from environment variables. This page describes what is created and which features can be enabled.

Bootstrap runs once

Bootstrap only runs when both the configuration and data directories are empty. OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_* variables are ignored on an existing directory. See How It Works.

docs.title: What Is Created
docs.text:
With default settings, bootstrap creates:

  • the global configuration, with size, time and idle limits;
  • the modules listed in OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MODULES;
  • the schemas listed in OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SCHEMAS (core, cosine, inetorgperson and rfc2307bis by default);
  • the configuration database, with its root DN cn=admin,cn=config;
  • one MDB data database for OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX, with its root DN cn=admin,<suffix>, indexes and access rules;
  • the monitor database;
  • the root entry of the directory, named after OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_ORGANIZATION.

Passwords are hashed with Argon2 (OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_FRONTEND_PASSWORD_HASH).

docs.title: Suffix and Organization
docs.text:
docker run --name openldap \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_ORGANIZATION="Keycloakers Org" \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX="dc=keycloakers,dc=org" \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX must start with dc=, in lowercase. Bootstrap stops with an error for any other suffix, such as o=acme.

Variables derived from the suffix follow it automatically: the data root DN becomes cn=admin,dc=keycloakers,dc=org.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
Each account password is taken from a *_PASSWORD_HASHED variable. When that variable is empty, a random password is generated, hashed, and printed once in the container logs:

docker logs openldap 2>&1 | grep -i password

To set a password yourself, hash it first and pass the hash:

docker run --rm osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- openldap-ctl password hash 'my-secret-password'

docker run --name openldap \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_ROOT_PASSWORD_HASHED='{ARGON2}$argon2id$v=19$m=7168,t=5,p=1$...' \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_CONFIG_ROOT_PASSWORD_HASHED='{ARGON2}$argon2id$v=19$m=7168,t=5,p=1$...' \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

Warning

Hashes contain $ characters. Use single quotes in a shell, and double every $ ($$) in a Docker Compose file.

docs.title: Optional Features
docs.text:
All optional features are disabled by default and enabled with one variable.

Feature Variable Documentation Users/groups/services branches OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_TREE=true Access Control Directory administrator OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_ADMIN=true Access Control Application management account OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_MANAGEMENT=true Access Control Read-only data account OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_READONLY=true Access Control Read-only monitor account OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MONITOR_READONLY=true Access Control Password policy OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_PPOLICY=true Overlays Referential integrity OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REFINT=true Overlays Unique attributes OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_UNIQUE=true Overlays Reverse group membership OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MEMBEROF=true Overlays TLS OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS=true TLS TLS required OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_TLS_REQUIRED=true TLS Multi-provider replication OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION=true Replication

docs.title: Indexes
docs.text:
The data database is created with these indexes:

Attributes Index objectClass eq uid, mail, cn, sn, givenName eq,sub member, uniqueMember eq entryCSN, entryUUID eq

The maximum database size is set by OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_DATABASE_MAX_SIZE (10 GB by default).

To change indexes or any other part of the generated configuration, see Custom LDIF.

docs.title: Going Further
docs.text:
• Access Control: who can read and write what.
  • Overlays: password policy, referential integrity, uniqueness, memberOf.
  • Schemas: schemas shipped with the image and how to add yours.
  • Custom LDIF: add, replace or remove any part of the bootstrap.

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text: Bootstrap creates a closed-by-default set of access rules (ACLs). Anything that is not explicitly allowed is denied.

docs.title: Who Can Do What
docs.text:
On the data database, with default settings:

Identity Access Data root DN (cn=admin,<suffix>) Full access ldap user through ldapi:/// Full access (manage) Authenticated user Reads a short list of attributes on every entry; changes their own password Anonymous Can only authenticate (bind); cannot read anything Directory admin (optional) Manages users/groups and resets user passwords; cannot read password hashes or manage service accounts Management account (optional) Reads users/groups and resets user passwords; cannot read password hashes or edit other attributes Read-only account (optional) Reads everything except passwords and, with ppolicy, password history Replication account (optional) Reads everything, including passwords

docs.title: Authenticated Users
docs.text:
Any authenticated user can read these attributes, on their own entry and on others:

objectClass, cn, sn, givenName, mail, uid, ou, o, dc

Other attributes are hidden, including on the user's own entry. A user can change their own userPassword.

Note

Applications that need more than this list, such as group membership or POSIX attributes, should bind with the read-only account instead.

docs.title: Local Administration
docs.text:
Inside the container, the ldap user has full access to the data and monitor databases through the local socket, without a password:

docker exec openldap container run -- \
  ldapsearch -Q -Y EXTERNAL -H ldapi:/// -b "dc=example,dc=org"

The configuration database (cn=config) is only accessible with its root DN, cn=admin,cn=config, and its password.

docs.title: Read-Only Data Account
docs.text:
Set OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_READONLY=true to create an account that can read the whole data database except userPassword and shadowLastChange. It is intended for applications that look up users and groups.

docker run --name openldap \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_READONLY=true \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc
Variable Default OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_READONLY_DN cn=readonly,${OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX} OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_READONLY_PASSWORD_HASHED empty: a password is generated and logged

When ppolicy is enabled, the account is also denied access to pwdHistory. Existing directories need an explicit ACL update to gain this restriction.

docs.title: Directory Administrator
docs.text:
Use this account for day-to-day administration, including login to phpLDAPadmin 2. It has a real directory entry; the data root DN is a virtual identity and cannot log in to phpLDAPadmin 2.

On a fresh installation:

docker run --name openldap \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_TREE=true \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_ADMIN=true \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

The default DN is cn=admin,ou=services,dc=example,dc=org. Supply its hash with OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_ADMIN_PASSWORD_HASHED, or use the generated password printed at bootstrap.

The administrator can create, edit, rename and delete users/groups and reset user passwords. It cannot read password hashes/history, access cn=config, or change service accounts, including its own. Use the data root to rotate its password.

docs.title: Management Account
docs.text:
Use this account for an application that looks up users/groups and resets user passwords, such as Authelia or Keycloak. Enable OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_TREE=true and OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_MANAGEMENT=true on a fresh installation.

The default DN is cn=management,ou=services,dc=example,dc=org. Supply its hash with OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_MANAGEMENT_PASSWORD_HASHED. It cannot edit profiles/groups or read password hashes/history with the default hidden-attribute settings.

Tree and account creation are independent. If you create the branches through custom LDIF, create their parent entries before the account fragments run.

Admin and management password resets bypass LDAP password quality, history and minimum-age checks. Enforce the required password policy in the application performing the reset.

For complete Helm setups with these accounts, see Authelia and Keycloak examples.

docs.title: Monitor Database
docs.text:
The monitor database (cn=Monitor) is always created. OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MONITOR sets its olcMonitoring value.

Set OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MONITOR_READONLY=true to create an account that can read it, for example for a metrics exporter:

Variable Default OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MONITOR_READONLY_DN cn=readonly-monitor,${OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SUFFIX} OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MONITOR_READONLY_PASSWORD_HASHED empty: a password is generated and logged

docs.title: Default Rules
docs.text:
These are the base rules, plus read-only and replication rules when enabled. Scoped admin and management rules run before them when those accounts are enabled.

olcAccess: to *
  by dn.exact="gidNumber=911+uidNumber=911,cn=peercred,cn=external,cn=auth" manage
  by * break
olcAccess: to attrs=userPassword,shadowLastChange
  by self write
  by anonymous auth
  by * break
olcAccess: to attrs=entry,objectClass,cn,sn,givenName,mail,uid,ou,o,dc
  by self read
  by users read
  by * break
# read-only account, when enabled
olcAccess: to attrs=userPassword,shadowLastChange
  by dn.exact="cn=readonly,dc=example,dc=org" none
  by * break
olcAccess: to *
  by dn.exact="cn=readonly,dc=example,dc=org" read
  by * break
# replication account, when enabled
olcAccess: to *
  by dn.exact="cn=replicator,dc=example,dc=org" read
  by * break
# final rule
olcAccess: to *
  by * none

Schema dependencies

The default rules reference mail (from cosine.ldif) and shadowLastChange (from rfc2307bis.ldif). If you remove one of these schemas from OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SCHEMAS, replace the default rules as described below.

docs.title: Changing the Rules
docs.text:
Access rules are built from separate LDIF fragments, so one part can be changed without rewriting the others:

Fragment Content 61-database-admin-ppolicy-acl.ldif.optional.template Hide password history from the directory admin when ppolicy is enabled 62-database-admin-acl.ldif.template Scoped directory administrator 63-database-management-acl.ldif.template Scoped management account 64-database-readonly-ppolicy-acl.ldif.optional.template Hide password history from the read-only account 65-database-acl.ldif.template Local administration, passwords, basic attributes 66-database-readonly-acl.ldif.template Read-only account 67-database-replication-acl.ldif.template Replication account 69-database-acl-close.ldif Final deny-all rule

To change the default rules before first start, replace 65-database-acl.ldif.template with your own file. See Custom LDIF.

On an existing directory, change olcAccess on olcDatabase={1}mdb,cn=config with ldapmodify, bound as the configuration root DN.

docs.title: Custom LDIF
docs.text: The whole bootstrap is built from small LDIF fragments. You can add your own, replace a built-in one, or remove it, without rebuilding the image.

docs.title: Custom Directories
docs.text:
Directory inside the container Content /container/services/openldap-bootstrap/assets/ldif/config/custom Configuration (cn=config): ACLs, indexes, overlays and other settings /container/services/openldap-bootstrap/assets/ldif/data/custom Initial directory entries: users, groups and other LDAP data

Create local directories and mount them into the container:

mkdir -p custom-config custom-data

docker run --name openldap \
  -v "$(pwd)/custom-config:/container/services/openldap-bootstrap/assets/ldif/config/custom" \
  -v "$(pwd)/custom-data:/container/services/openldap-bootstrap/assets/ldif/data/custom" \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

Put .ldif files in these directories, or .ldif.template files with ${VARIABLE} placeholders that are replaced by environment variables. Leave the mounts writable so bootstrap can convert templates into .ldif files.

Note

Custom files are only used by bootstrap, on first start. They do not change an existing directory.

docs.title: Add Content
docs.text:
Use a new file name. For example, custom-data/70-users.ldif:

dn: ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: organizationalUnit
ou: people

dn: uid=jdoe,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org
objectClass: inetOrgPerson
uid: jdoe
cn: John Doe
sn: Doe
mail: jdoe@example.org

Each entry needs a dn: and its required attributes, with a blank line between entries. Parent entries must come before their children.

Entries are imported with slapadd: write plain entries, without modification instructions such as changetype: modify.

docs.title: Replace a Built-In Fragment
docs.text:
Copy the built-in file into the matching custom directory, keep the file name, and edit it.

For example, to change the default access rules, copy 65-database-acl.ldif.template into custom-config/ and edit it. To change database settings and indexes, do the same with 60-database.ldif.template.

Replacing one fragment leaves the others in place: replacing 65-database-acl.ldif.template keeps the final deny-all rule from 69-database-acl-close.ldif and the rules added by enabled features such as the read-only account or replication.

docs.title: Remove a Built-In Fragment
docs.text: Provide an empty .ldif file with the same output file name. For example, an empty custom-config/65-database-acl.ldif removes the rules from 65-database-acl.ldif.template.

docs.title: How Fragments Are Assembled
docs.text:
Files are sorted by their numeric prefix, then concatenated into one LDIF file per database. Prefixes are grouped by tens:

  • Files in the same ten-group (for example 60-* and 65-*) are concatenated without a blank line: they form a single entry.
  • When the ten-group changes (for example 69-* to 70-*), one blank line is inserted: a new entry starts.
  • Leading and trailing empty lines are removed from every file.

This is how several files build one entry. The data database entry is assembled from:

File Adds 60-database.ldif.template The entry itself, with its indexes 61-database-replication.ldif.template Replication settings, when enabled 61-… to 64-… Scoped admin/management rules and password-history restrictions, when enabled 65-database-acl.ldif.template Default access rules 66-… and 67-… Access rules of optional accounts 69-database-acl-close.ldif Final deny-all rule

So a custom file named 62-my-indexes.ldif containing only olcDbIndex: lines adds indexes to the data database, while a file named 200-my-overlay.ldif starts a new entry.

File names without a numeric prefix, such as users.ldif, are accepted. Each one forms its own group.

docs.title: Built-In Fragments
docs.text:
Configuration fragments, in config/base:

File Description 00-global.ldif.template Global limits (size, time, idle timeout) 10-module.ldif.template Module path and module list 20-schema.ldif Schema container 30-schema-import.ldif.template Schemas to load 40-frontend.ldif.template Frontend database (password hash scheme) 50-config.ldif.template Configuration database, root DN and password 59-config-acl-close.ldif Deny-all rule on the configuration database 60-database.ldif.template Data database (MDB) with indexes 65-database-acl.ldif.template Data database access rules 69-database-acl-close.ldif Deny-all rule on the data database 70-monitor.ldif.template Monitor database 75-monitor-acl.ldif.template Monitor database access rules 79-monitor-acl-close.ldif Deny-all rule on the monitor database

Optional features add their own fragments: 01- and 02- for TLS, 03-, 61-, 67- and 180- for replication, 61- to 64- for scoped admin/management and password-history restrictions, 66- and 76- for read-only accounts, 100- to 170- for overlays. Data fragments include 30-data-tree.ldif, 70-database-admin-account.ldif and 80-database-management-account.ldif.

Overlays are created in prefix order, and the order matters. Keep syncprov last, as with the built-in 180- prefix.

The complete list is in the LDIF directory of the repository.

docs.title: Overlays
docs.text:
Four common OpenLDAP overlays can be enabled at bootstrap. Each one is disabled by default and is added to the data database when its variable is set to true.

The default OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MODULES=auto loads the modules needed for the enabled features. You can also supply an explicit ordered list.

docker run --name openldap \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_PPOLICY=true \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REFINT=true \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_UNIQUE=true \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MEMBEROF=true \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

docs.title: Password Policy
docs.text:
OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_PPOLICY=true enables the ppolicy overlay and creates a default policy applied to every account.

Bootstrap creates two entries in the data database:

  • a container, ou=policies,<suffix> (OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_PPOLICY_GROUP_DN);
  • the default policy, cn=default,ou=policies,<suffix> (OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_PPOLICY_DEFAULT_POLICY_DN).

The default policy is:

Setting Default Variable suffix (OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_PPOLICY_DEFAULT_…) Minimum length 12 characters MIN_LENGTH Check password quality when possible (1) CHECK_QUALITY Password history 12 passwords IN_HISTORY Maximum age 90 days MAX_AGE Expiration warning 14 days before EXPIRE_WARNING Grace logins after expiration 3 GRACE_AUTH_NLIMIT Lockout after 5 failures LOCKOUT, MAX_FAILURE Failure counter reset 5 minutes FAILURE_COUNT_INTERVAL Lockout duration 15 minutes LOCKOUT_DURATION Progressive lockout disabled (0) MIN_DELAY, MAX_DELAY Maximum inactivity disabled (0) MAX_IDLE Users can change their password yes ALLOW_USER_CHANGE Old password required to change yes SAFE_MODIFY Must change after admin reset no MUST_CHANGE

Durations are set in seconds. Overlay-level settings are OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_PPOLICY_HASH_CLEAR_TEXT, OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_PPOLICY_USE_LOCKOUT and OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_PPOLICY_CHECK_MODULE.

See Environment Variables for every setting.

docs.title: Progressive lockout and inactivity
docs.text:
For a short lockout after each failed bind, set OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_PPOLICY_DEFAULT_MIN_DELAY and MAX_DELAY to positive seconds, with MIN_DELAY <= MAX_DELAY. Keep policy lockout enabled.

To block accounts after a period without successful authentication, enable OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_LAST_BIND=true and set OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_PPOLICY_DEFAULT_MAX_IDLE in seconds. This also requires policy lockout. OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_DATA_LAST_BIND_PRECISION controls how often successful binds update the timestamp (default: one hour).

These options apply on first bootstrap. Changing environment variables does not update an existing policy or server configuration.

docs.title: Referential Integrity
docs.text:
OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REFINT=true enables the refint overlay. When an entry is renamed or deleted, references to it are updated or removed in other entries, so groups do not keep members that no longer exist.

Variable Default OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REFINT_ATTRIBUTES member uniqueMember manager owner OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REFINT_NOTHING_DN empty

Set OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REFINT_NOTHING_DN to a placeholder DN if deleting the last member would leave a group invalid. Bootstrap creates a passwordless role at that DN; its parent must exist.

docs.title: Unique Attributes
docs.text:
OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_UNIQUE=true enables the unique overlay, which rejects an entry when another entry already has the same value for a given attribute.

Variable Default OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_UNIQUE_URIS ldap:///?uid?sub ldap:///?mail?sub

With the default value, uid and mail are unique across the whole directory.

docs.title: MemberOf
docs.text:
OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MEMBEROF=true enables the memberof overlay, which maintains a memberOf attribute on each member of a group.

Variable Default Description OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MEMBEROF_GROUP_OC groupOfNames Object class treated as a group OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MEMBEROF_MEMBER_AD member Membership attribute watched on groups OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MEMBEROF_MEMBEROF_AD memberOf Reverse attribute maintained on members OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MEMBEROF_ADD_CHECK true Check new entries against existing groups OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MEMBEROF_DANGLING ignore Handling of members that do not exist

Note

memberOf is not in the list of attributes readable by authenticated users. Applications should read it with the read-only account.

When replication is also enabled, memberOf is excluded from replication and computed locally on each server.

docs.title: Overlay Order
docs.text:
Overlays are created in this order: ppolicy, unique, refint, memberof, then syncprov when replication is enabled.

To add another overlay or change the order, see Custom LDIF. Keep syncprov last.

docs.title: Schemas
docs.text:
Schemas are loaded at bootstrap from the list in OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SCHEMAS. Each name is a file in /etc/openldap/schema, in cn=config LDIF format.

The default list is:

OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SCHEMAS="core.ldif cosine.ldif inetorgperson.ldif rfc2307bis.ldif"

docs.title: Loading More Schemas
docs.text:
Add the schema file names to the list, after the schemas they depend on:

docker run --name openldap \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SCHEMAS="core.ldif cosine.ldif inetorgperson.ldif rfc2307bis.ldif openssh-lpk.ldif sudo.ldif" \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

Warning

The default access rules reference attributes from cosine.ldif and rfc2307bis.ldif. Keep these two schemas in the list, or replace the default rules.

docs.title: Schemas Shipped With the Image
docs.text:
In addition to the schemas provided by OpenLDAP (core, cosine, inetorgperson, nis, dyngroup, misc and others), the image ships these:

Schema Purpose rfc2307bis.ldif UNIX accounts and groups, with better group modeling than nis eduperson.ldif Academic identities used in higher-education federations kerberos.ldif Kerberos principals for LDAP-backed KDC setups openssh-lpk.ldif SSH public keys (sshPublicKey) postfix-book.ldif Mail accounts and forwards, as used by docker-mailserver virtualMail.ldif Virtual mailbox deployments samba.ldif Samba domain and account attributes sudo.ldif Sudo rules (sudoRole) totp.ldif TOTP secrets for LDAP-based two-factor authentication

Incompatible schemas

  • Do not load postfix-book.ldif together with virtualMail.ldif: they define attributes with the same names but different OIDs.
  • rfc2307bis.ldif replaces nis.ldif: load one or the other.

Sources are listed in the schema directory of the repository.

docs.title: Adding Your Own Schema
docs.text:
Custom schemas are read from /container/services/openldap/assets/schema and copied to the OpenLDAP schema directory at startup.

1. Convert the schema to LDIF if it is in the traditional .schema format:

docker run --rm --user $UID -v $(pwd)/schema:/data \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- openldap-ctl schema2ldif /data/my-app.schema

This writes my-app.ldif next to the source file. See LDAP Toolkit.

2. Mount the LDIF file and add it to the list:

docker run --name openldap \
  -v $(pwd)/schema/my-app.ldif:/container/services/openldap/assets/schema/my-app.ldif \
  -e OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_SCHEMAS="core.ldif cosine.ldif inetorgperson.ldif rfc2307bis.ldif my-app.ldif" \
  osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc

To add a schema to an existing directory, load the LDIF file with ldapadd bound as the configuration root DN.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
By default, OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MODULES=auto loads the modules needed by enabled features. To choose modules yourself, supply an ordered list, for example:

OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_MODULES="back_mdb.so argon2.so ppolicy.so unique.so refint.so memberof.so syncprov.so"

The image includes all OpenLDAP backends and overlays, plus the Argon2, PBKDF2 and SHA-2 password modules. When using an explicit list, include the modules needed by your configured database, password hash and overlays.

To use a module that is not part of the image, mount it in /container/services/openldap/assets/module: it is copied to the OpenLDAP modules directory at startup.

docs.title: Helm charts
docs.text:
Deploy OpenLDAP and phpLDAPadmin on Kubernetes with the Osixia charts.

Chart What it provides openldap An LDAP directory with persistent storage, TLS, replication and optional scheduled backups phpldapadmin A web interface for managing LDAP users and groups

docs.title: Add the repository
docs.text:
helm repo add osixia https://charts.opensource.osixia.net
helm repo update osixia
helm search repo osixia

Follow the OpenLDAP guide to prepare values and install a directory, then add phpLDAPadmin if you want a web interface.

The guides follow the source charts: OpenLDAP chart 0.3.0 targets osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc; phpLDAPadmin chart 0.2.1 targets phpldapadmin/phpldapadmin:2.3.11. Check helm search repo osixia --versions for published versions.

docs.title: Use a local checkout
docs.text:
To use source changes before they are published:

git clone https://github.com/osixia/helm-charts.git
cd helm-charts

Use ./openldap or ./phpldapadmin as the chart path in place of osixia/openldap or osixia/phpldapadmin.

For a working stack with generated credentials and verified StartTLS, see the Authelia and Keycloak examples.

Source code and complete values

docs.title: 🎮 LDAP with Authelia or Keycloak
docs.text:
The chart repository contains two ready-to-try stacks. Each creates its own namespace, credentials and local CA, and uses verified StartTLS between the applications and OpenLDAP.

Example What you get Authelia OpenLDAP, phpLDAPadmin and the official Authelia chart Keycloak OpenLDAP, phpLDAPadmin, the community keycloakx chart with the official Keycloak image, and PostgreSQL

docs.title: Try one
docs.text:
You need Helm 3, kubectl, Python 3, OpenSSL and a cluster with dynamic volume provisioning. The OpenLDAP image used by the example must be available to your cluster.

git clone https://github.com/osixia/helm-charts.git
cd helm-charts/examples/ldap-stack-authelia
python3 prepare.py

Then follow that example's README to create the namespace, apply the generated resources and install the releases. For Keycloak, use examples/ldap-stack-keycloak instead.

The generator creates a private generated/ directory containing credentials, Secrets and certificates. Read generated/credentials.json for the passwords. It refuses to overwrite an existing directory. These examples are for a fresh installation: regenerating a Secret does not rotate passwords in an existing directory or database.

docs.title: Understand the accounts
docs.text:
Account Purpose Data and config roots LDAP maintenance and recovery Directory admin Log in to phpLDAPadmin and manage users/groups Application bind account Read users/groups and change user passwords for Authelia or Keycloak Alice Sample user for trying login flows

Application bind accounts cannot read password hashes or edit profiles/groups. Their privileged password resets bypass LDAP quality and history checks, so configure a matching password policy in the application.

docs.title: Before adapting it for real users
docs.text:
Replace the local CA and sample users, configure your public HTTPS hostnames, and set up backups. Authelia needs a real notifier for emails; Keycloak needs its own SMTP settings and database backup. Neither example enables MFA for you.

Each README also includes a reproducible integration test using a disposable kind cluster, covering login flows, password changes, LDAP access rules and StartTLS verification.

docs.title: 🪪 OpenLDAP
docs.text:
This chart runs osixia/openldap as a StatefulSet. The quickstart below installs a test directory with one replica and persistent storage. For network access, prepare TLS before installing.

You need Helm 3, kubectl, and a cluster with dynamic volume provisioning, or your own volume configuration.

docs.title: 1. Prepare passwords
docs.text:
Generate two different passwords and hashes, one for the data root and one for the configuration root:

docker run --rm osixia/openldap:2.6.15-rc run -- openldap-ctl password generate

Run the command twice. Keep the passwords somewhere safe and put their {ARGON2}... hashes in my-values.yaml:

openldap:
  bootstrap:
    organization: My Org
    suffix: dc=example,dc=org
    database:
      rootPasswordHashed: "{ARGON2}..."
    config:
      rootPasswordHashed: "{ARGON2}..."

These values initialize an empty directory. Changing them later does not rotate passwords in an existing database.

docs.title: 2. Install and connect
docs.text:
After adding the chart repository:

helm install my-ldap osixia/openldap \
  --namespace directory --create-namespace -f my-values.yaml --wait
kubectl -n directory get pods,pvc

The LDAP address inside the cluster is my-ldap-openldap.directory.svc.cluster.local:389 with the default cluster domain. For a local check:

kubectl -n directory port-forward svc/my-ldap-openldap 1389:389
ldapsearch -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:1389 \
  -D 'cn=admin,dc=example,dc=org' -W -b 'dc=example,dc=org'

The initial setup has TLS disabled. Enable it before sending credentials over the network.

docs.title: TLS for a new installation
docs.text:
Before your first installation, create the directory namespace if it does not exist (kubectl create namespace directory). Then create a Secret containing your server certificate, private key and CA certificate. The certificate must cover the DNS names clients use:

kubectl -n directory create secret generic ldap-tls \
  --from-file=tls.crt=certs/tls.crt \
  --from-file=tls.key=certs/tls.key \
  --from-file=ca.crt=certs/ca.crt

Add these values before the first installation:

tlsSecret:
  existingSecret: ldap-tls

openldap:
  tlsReload:
    enabled: true
  bootstrap:
    tls:
      enabled: true
      required: true

Merge them into your existing values under the same openldap key. Clients can use StartTLS on service port 389 or LDAPS on 636, and must trust your CA. The TLS reload sidecar restarts the OpenLDAP process when certificate contents change; the pod stays running, but LDAP connections can be interrupted briefly.

On an existing directory, bootstrap values do not reconfigure TLS. Update the live cn=config settings first; see the container TLS guide.

docs.title: Storage and backups
docs.text:
Persistence is enabled by default, with separate volumes for configuration (1Gi), data (8Gi) and backups (8Gi). Set persistence.storageClass if the cluster has no default StorageClass. A custom persistence.<name>.volume overrides generated storage for that volume.

To enable the daily backup job:

backupCronJob:
  enabled: true
  schedule: "15 2 * * *"

The job uses pod 0's volumes and runs on the same node. Its default command keeps scheduled backups for 15 days and preserves manual and upgrade backups. Copy backups to separate storage as part of your backup process.

For manual backup and restore commands, see Backup / Restore.

docs.title: More than one replica
docs.text:
The chart enables replication automatically when replicaCount is greater than one, unless you override the replication mode. Supply the same plaintext replication password to every replica, preferably through bootstrapEnvSecret.existingSecret using OPENLDAP_BOOTSTRAP_REPLICATION_DATA_READONLY_PASSWORD.

Choose the replica count at installation. Changing it later is guarded because the generated replication hosts are stored in the directory; changing a value alone does not safely reconfigure replication.

docs.title: Upgrade
docs.text:
For an upgrade with the default pre-upgrade step enabled, set previousImage.tag to the image currently running:

previousImage:
  tag: 2.6.15-beta  # example: replace with your currently running image tag
image:
  tag: 2.6.15-rc

helm upgrade my-ldap osixia/openldap -n directory -f my-values.yaml --wait

The old image creates a migration backup before the new image starts. Remove previousImage.tag from your values after the upgrade. A fresh install does not need it. Moving from the v1 image requires a manual migration.

For scoped accounts, replication settings and the full values reference, see the chart README.

docs.title: 🖥️ phpLDAPadmin
docs.text: Add a web interface to an existing LDAP directory. This chart uses phpLDAPadmin 2; it does not install an LDAP server.

docs.title: Connect to your directory
docs.text:
Save this as phpldapadmin-values.yaml, adjusting the host and base DN:

app:
  ldap:
    host: my-ldap-openldap.directory.svc.cluster.local
    port: 389
    connection: starttls
    tls: true

extraEnv:
  - name: LDAP_BASE_DN
    value: dc=example,dc=org
  - name: LDAP_LOGIN_ATTR
    value: dn
  - name: LDAP_LOGIN_OBJECTCLASS
    value: organizationalRole
  - name: LDAPTLS_CACERT
    value: /ldap-ca/ca.crt
  - name: LDAPTLS_REQCERT
    value: demand

extraEnvFrom:
  - secretRef:
      name: ldap-admin-bind

extraVolumes:
  - name: ldap-ca
    secret:
      secretName: ldap-tls
extraVolumeMounts:
  - name: ldap-ca
    mountPath: /ldap-ca
    readOnly: true

This assumes OpenLDAP has TLS enabled and the ldap-tls Secret contains ca.crt in the same namespace. The LDAP hostname must match the server certificate. Here, tls: true enables StartTLS on port 389. For LDAPS, use port 636, connection: ldaps, ssl: true and tls: false.

phpLDAPadmin 2 needs a real directory entry to log in. The OpenLDAP data root (cn=admin,<suffix>) is a virtual identity and cannot log in. Create a scoped directory administrator before the first OpenLDAP installation by adding these values alongside your existing bootstrap settings:

openldap:
  bootstrap:
    database:
      tree:
        enabled: true
      admin:
        enabled: true
        passwordHashed: "{ARGON2}..."

Generate a separate password/hash for this account as in the OpenLDAP guide. Put its plaintext password in a local file named admin-password.txt, without a trailing newline, then create the search-credentials Secret:

kubectl -n directory create secret generic ldap-admin-bind \
  --from-literal=LDAP_USERNAME='cn=admin,ou=services,dc=example,dc=org' \
  --from-file=LDAP_PASSWORD=admin-password.txt

The same administrator is used for search and login here. For a complete setup with generated credentials, use the application examples.

docs.title: Install and open
docs.text:
After adding the chart repository:

helm install ldap-admin osixia/phpldapadmin \
  -n directory -f phpldapadmin-values.yaml --wait
kubectl -n directory port-forward svc/ldap-admin-phpldapadmin 8080:80

Open http://localhost:8080 and log in with cn=admin,ou=services,dc=example,dc=org and its password. The service exposes port 80 and forwards to the image's port 8080.

docs.title: Useful settings
docs.text:
Value What it controls app.ldap.host, port, tls, ssl LDAP endpoint and transport extraEnv, extraEnvFrom Additional application settings and credentials from Secrets app.existingSecret Existing Secret containing APP_KEY ingress.enabled Expose through a Kubernetes Ingress httpRoute.enabled Expose through Gateway API; requires its CRDs and a compatible controller

The chart generates a stable APP_KEY across upgrades if you do not supply one. Expose the web interface over HTTPS when accessing it remotely.

docs.title: kube-network-detector
docs.text:
Find which Kubernetes node receives traffic for a virtual IP, or which nodes can reach a TCP endpoint. The detector records the result as node labels, which you can use in pod scheduling rules.

It runs on each node as a DaemonSet, using the node's network (hostNetwork: true). IPv4 and IPv6 are supported.

docs.title: Two things it can check
docs.text:
Check What happens Example label VIP routing An elected observer probes the VIP and identifies the responding node kube-network-detector/203.0.113.10=true Peer connectivity Each node tries a TCP connection to a named IP and port kube-network-detector/peer-database.default=true for a Peer named database in namespace default

You can use either check or both. A successful TCP connection means the endpoint is reachable; it does not check application health.

By default, two consecutive successes add a label and three consecutive failures remove it. Other node labels are left alone.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Quickstart: install the DaemonSet and declare your first target.
  • Configuration: change probe timing, use static targets or enable dry-run.
  • Troubleshooting: investigate missing labels and failed probes.

The detector observes routing. It does not configure interfaces, move VIPs or set up your firewall.

Source code and full reference

docs.title: Targets in Kubernetes
docs.text:
The detector watches VIP and Peer objects across all namespaces by default. Adding, changing or deleting an object takes effect without restarting the DaemonSet. The object's namespace must already exist.

Target Required spec fields Default node label VIP address kube-network-detector/<IP>=true Peer address, port kube-network-detector/peer-<name>.<namespace>=true

For IPv6 VIPs, the suffix is ipv6- followed by the address's 32 hexadecimal digits. For example, 2001:db8::1 becomes ipv6-20010db8000000000000000000000001. Long Peer identities use a hash; check the logs for the resulting label.

Deleted or changed CRD targets have their obsolete labels cleaned up by each running instance on its own node. API errors retain the last known configuration. Instances that were offline clean up when they return in CRD mode.

docs.title: Useful settings
docs.text:
Set these in the DaemonSet container's args:

Flag Default Use it to… --interval 5s Change the time between probes --timeout 2s Allow more or less time for a connection --success-threshold 2 Require more successes before adding a label --failure-threshold 3 Require more failures before removing a label --port 9876 Change the VIP responder port on every node --vip-label-prefix kube-network-detector/ Change the start of VIP label keys --peer-label-prefix kube-network-detector/peer- Change the start of Peer label keys --dry-run false Log proposed changes without writing labels or Leases

For example, use --timeout=5s for a slower network. Keep keys, ports, prefixes and CRD mode consistent across pods.

Flags also accept environment variables: --timeout becomes KUBE_NETWORK_DETECTOR_TIMEOUT. Explicit flags win over environment variables.

Logging uses --log-level and --log-format, or CONTAINER_LOG_LEVEL and CONTAINER_LOG_FORMAT. Use --log-level=debug when investigating a problem.

docs.title: Static targets
docs.text:
To configure targets directly in the DaemonSet instead of using CRDs:

args:
  - --disable-crds
  - --peers=database=10.0.0.20:5432,api=[2001:db8::1]:443

This peer-only configuration needs the node name and Node get/patch permissions. It needs no HMAC key, responder or Lease permissions. If adapting the supplied manifest, remove the responder's readiness/liveness probes and port configuration too: there is no listening server in this mode.

A static peer named database uses kube-network-detector/peer-database, without a namespace suffix.

For VIPs, also add --vips=203.0.113.10,2001:db8::1 and keep the shared key, responder and Lease permissions. VIPs need Node get/list/patch and Lease get/create/update permissions. The supplied manifest includes these.

Keep the Downward API identity variables from the supplied manifest:

Variable Source Needed for KUBE_NETWORK_DETECTOR_NODE_NAME spec.nodeName All modes KUBE_NETWORK_DETECTOR_POD_NAMESPACE metadata.namespace VIPs or CRD discovery KUBE_NETWORK_DETECTOR_POD_UID metadata.uid VIPs or CRD discovery

Without --disable-crds, static targets and CRD targets are combined.

docs.title: Try changes without writing labels
docs.text:
Set --dry-run=true on every pod. Probes still run and proposed changes appear in the logs, but the detector writes no labels, inventory annotations or Leases. VIP observers probe without leader election in this mode.

During a rollout, pods still using --dry-run=false can continue to write changes.

docs.title: Updates and cleanup
docs.text:
Changing DaemonSet arguments triggers a rollout. If you change the HMAC Secret, restart the pods so they load it again:

kubectl -n kube-network-detector rollout restart daemonset/kube-network-detector
kubectl -n kube-network-detector rollout status daemonset/kube-network-detector

Only one HMAC key is supported at a time. Mixed keys during rotation can cause failed probes and label removal.

Static targets leave their labels behind when removed. After every pod uses the new configuration, remove each obsolete label explicitly, for example:

kubectl label nodes --all kube-network-detector/peer-database-

Shutdown also leaves labels in place. Keep CRD mode running until deleted targets have been cleaned up; switching it off does not clean old CRD labels. Avoid multiple deployments managing the same labels or sharing the CRD inventory annotation on the same nodes.

Full CLI and Go library reference

docs.title: ⚡ Quickstart
docs.text: This guide installs the detector and checks connectivity to a database. Add the optional VIP target if you also want to detect which node receives traffic for a virtual IP.

docs.title: 1. Get the manifest
docs.text:
You need kubectl, access to create CRDs and cluster RBAC, and a cluster that allows hostNetwork. The supplied CRDs require Kubernetes 1.30 or newer.

git clone https://github.com/osixia/kube-network-detector.git
cd kube-network-detector

Open docs/examples/kubernetes/kube-network-detector.yaml and replace the example Secret's stringData.hmac-key with a new key:

openssl rand -hex 32

Use an image built from the same source revision as the manifest, with CRD discovery support. Set the manifest's image field to the matching tag or digest before deploying.

All detector pods must use the same key. The default installation starts a VIP responder even if you only declare Peer objects, so it still needs this key and a free TCP port 9876 on each node. For peer-only operation without a responder, see static targets.

docs.title: 2. Install
docs.text:
kubectl apply -f docs/examples/kubernetes/kube-network-detector.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established --timeout=60s \
  crd/vips.network.cloud.osixia.net crd/peers.network.cloud.osixia.net
kubectl -n kube-network-detector rollout status daemonset/kube-network-detector

The manifest installs the CRDs, Secret, RBAC and DaemonSet. It creates no targets yet.

docs.title: 3. Add a target
docs.text:
Save this as my-targets.yaml. Replace 10.0.0.20 and 5432 with your database's IP and TCP port:

apiVersion: network.cloud.osixia.net/v1alpha1
kind: Peer
metadata:
  name: database
  namespace: default
spec:
  address: 10.0.0.20
  port: 5432

kubectl apply -f my-targets.yaml
kubectl get nodes -L kube-network-detector/peer-database.default

After two successful probes, nodes that can connect show true. The default probe interval is five seconds; allow a few cycles for discovery and confirmation.

To check a VIP too, save this as my-vip.yaml, using a VIP that your network already routes to a node:

apiVersion: network.cloud.osixia.net/v1alpha1
kind: VIP
metadata:
  name: gateway
  namespace: default
spec:
  address: 203.0.113.10

kubectl apply -f my-vip.yaml
kubectl get nodes -L kube-network-detector/203.0.113.10

An observer whose interfaces do not have the VIP must be able to reach it on TCP port 9876. A node with the VIP on a local interface responds to probes but cannot observe that VIP itself. Do not put a Service or ingress in front of the probe port: the probe must reach the actual node through the VIP.

docs.title: 4. Use the label
docs.text:
For example, add this to a pod's spec to schedule it on a node that can reach the database:

nodeSelector:
  kube-network-detector/peer-database.default: "true"

The scheduler uses the label when placing the pod. Removing it later does not evict a pod that is already running.

Read Configuration for dry-run and cleanup, or Troubleshooting if no labels appear.

docs.title: 🩺 Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start with the pods and logs:

kubectl -n kube-network-detector get pods -o wide
kubectl -n kube-network-detector logs \
  -l app.kubernetes.io/name=kube-network-detector --prefix --tail=100

docs.title: The pod does not start
docs.text:
Check its events with kubectl -n kube-network-detector describe pod <pod-name>.

Message or symptom Check CRD missing or access forbidden Apply both CRDs and the supplied RBAC, or use --disable-crds for static targets Invalid HMAC key Use 64 hexadecimal characters, identical on every pod Address already in use Free port 9876, or change the responder port consistently across pods, container ports and health probes Admission rejection Check that the namespace allows hostNetwork No pod on a particular node Check the Linux node selector and tolerations; custom taints need matching tolerations

docs.title: A VIP has no label
docs.text:
• Check the address in the VIP object and allow a few probe cycles.
  • Make sure at least one detector node does not have the VIP on a local interface. Only those nodes can observe it.
  • Check routes and firewalls between that observer and the VIP on the responder port.
  • Check that all responders use the same key and that node clocks are synchronized.
  • Check Node patch and Lease permissions. API errors do not count as failed network probes.

A running pod and a passing TCP readiness probe only show that the responder accepts connections. They do not confirm correct VIP routing or successful label updates.

docs.title: A Peer has no label
docs.text:
Check the IP and TCP port from the affected node's network. The target does not need a detector, but it must accept a TCP connection.

Check the label name too: a CRD Peer named database in namespace default uses peer-database.default; a static peer named database uses peer-database.

docs.title: The wrong node is detected
docs.text: Inspect your routing, NAT, WireGuard setup and proxies. An address absent from local interfaces can still take a different path from public inbound traffic. A Service, NodePort or load balancer in front of the probe port can change which node answers.

docs.title: Old labels remain
docs.text:
Labels stay on shutdown. Static target removal and prefix changes need explicit cleanup; see Updates and cleanup.

For CRD targets, a running instance on the affected node must reconcile the deletion. A node that stays offline retains its labels until it returns.
